# idr_embed_divergence

Protein language model analyses of functional divergence among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).

## Overview

This repository contains code to reproduce selected analyses from **Using Protein Language Model Embeddings to Identify Intrinsically Disordered Regions Driving Protein Family Diversification** ([manuscript in preparation]). The project uses protein language model embeddings to investigate functional divergence among IDRs within protein families, including cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).

The code supports generating sequence embeddings, calculating neighbour distances and Family Neighbour Divergence (FND), inferring functional associations through Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment, and training IDR-LM.


## Contents

- [Repository structure](#repository-structure)
- [Installation](#installation)
- [Input data](#input-data)
- [Analysis workflows](#analysis-workflows)
- [Outputs](#outputs)
- [Reproducibility and known limitations](#reproducibility-and-known-limitations)
- [Contributions and acknowledgments](#contributions-and-acknowledgments)
- [Citation](#citation)
- [License](#license)

## Repository structure

| Location | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `src/idr_diverge/` | Core Python modules for embedding generation and downstream analyses. |
| `src/idr_diverge/IDR_LM_train/` | IDR-LM training code and model configuration files. |
| `scripts/` | Entry-point scripts for running workflows. |
| `configs/` | YAML configuration files specifying inputs, outputs, and analysis settings. |
| `envs/` | Conda environments and dependencies for different workflows |
| `data/` | Input datasets; see availability information below. |
| `res/` or `results/` | Output locations specified in configuration files. |
| `docs/` | Detailed workflow instructions. |

Detailed workflow instructions should be placed in `docs/`; proposed documentation filenames are listed below.

## Installation

The analyses were originally run on Linux. [Add the tested distribution/version and hardware requirements.]

### 1. Clone the repository

```bash
git clone <repo-link>
cd idr_embed_divergence
```

### 2. Create the analysis environment

```bash
conda env create -f envs/env.yml
conda activate diverge_env
pip install -e .
```

Run these commands from the repository root. The editable installation makes the `idr_diverge` package available to the workflow scripts.

### 3. Create workflow-specific environments as needed

For neighbour distance and FND analyses:

```bash
conda env create -f envs/fnd_env.yml
conda activate fnd_env
pip install -e .
```

For IDR-LM training:

```bash
conda env create -f envs/train_env.yml
conda activate lm_train
pip install -e .
```

## Input data

Workflows require some or all of the following:

- Protein or protein-segment sequences in FASTA format.
- Sequence embeddings in CSV or HDF5 (`.h5`) format, as supported by each script.
- Ortholog embeddings and, when filtering orthologs, an Ensembl homolog annotation file.
- A JSON mapping of protein-family names to UniProt IDs.
- A GO ontology file (`.obo`) and GO annotation table.
- A trained model checkpoint when generating embeddings with `IDR_LM`.

Most scripts expect sequence identifiers in the following format:

```text
{SPECIES_OR_ENSEMBL_ID}_{UNIPROT_ID}_{SEGMENT_TYPE}_{START}_{END}
```

Examples:

```text
HUMAN_Q14004_IDR_1_694
ENSNLEP00000006574_P12345_PFAM_45_120
```

Use consistent identifiers across related files. GO-enrichment query IDs must exactly match those in the embedding file.

Detailed specifications for identifiers, coordinate conventions, FASTA headers, and embedding formats belong in `docs/input-data.md` [to be added].


## Data availability

- **Toy datasets:** Small example inputs for testing the workflows are
  provided in `data/toy-data/`.
- **Processed examples:** Example processed datasets are provided in
  `data/examples/`.
- **Raw data:** Available from [Zenodo](YOUR_ZENODO_LINK). Includes annotation data, plm embeddings (human IDRs, human PFAM domains, CDK IDR and PFAM domain orthologs), IDR-LM training data, IDR-LM model weights and configs.


## Analysis workflows

Commands below assume that the entry-point scripts are located in `scripts/` and are run from the repository root. [Verify these paths against the repository.]

| Workflow | Purpose | Instructions |
|---|---|---|
| Data preparation | Prepare sequences, segment annotations, and protein families | [Data preparation](docs/data-preparation.md) |
| Embedding generation | Generate representations of IDRs and domains | [Embeddings](docs/embeddings.md) |
| Neighbour distance/divergence | Identify nearby segments in embedding space | [Nearest neighbours](docs/nearest-neighbours.md) |
| GO enrichment and similarity | Infer functional associations and compare enrichment profiles | [GO analysis](docs/go-analysis.md) |
| Family divergence | Calculate FND for protein families | [Family divergence](docs/family-divergence.md) |
| Visualization | Generate embedding visualizations and figures | [Visualization](docs/visualization.md) |

Each workflow document describes its required inputs, commands, parameters, and outputs.


### 1. Generate protein language model embeddings

Generate embeddings for sequences in a single FASTA file or a directory of FASTA files. Supported embedding types are:

- `esm`: ESM-1b.
- `IDR_LM`: trained IDR-LM; requires a model checkpoint.
- `IDR_LM_random`: randomly initialized IDR-LM.

```bash
python scripts/get_embeddings.py --config configs/embed_config.yaml
```

Set the embedding type, input path, output directory, and model/script paths in the configuration file. Paths in the embedding configuration are resolved relative to that configuration file.

**Output:** One HDF5 embedding file per input FASTA file.

**Detailed documentation:** `docs/embeddings.md`.

### 2. Calculate neighbour distances and FND

Compare neighbour distances between paralogous segments with an ortholog-based background. FND measures the difference between the average paralog neighbour distance and the expected ortholog/background neighbour distance.

**Required inputs:** Background embeddings, ortholog embeddings, and a family-to-UniProt mapping. An ortholog annotation file is also required when ortholog filtering is enabled. The family mapping is not required when running only the random-background calculation.

```bash
python scripts/run_ndivergence.py configs/ndist_config.yml
```

The configuration controls three analysis components:

1. `neighbour_divergence`: calculate neighbour distances between paralogous segments (`between`) or among orthologs of the same segment (`within`).
2. `random_neighbour_divergence`: estimate background divergence using orthologs of randomly sampled segments.
3. `calculate_FND`: combine family and background distance results to calculate FND.

For a staged run, generate the family and random-background distances first. Then set their output paths under `calculate_FND`, enable that component, and run the pipeline again. The configuration also supports recomputing background distances when no background distance file is supplied.

**Outputs:** Pickled neighbour-distance dictionaries and a CSV of FND results. Higher positive FND values indicate greater paralog divergence relative to the ortholog/background baseline.

**Detailed documentation:** `docs/divergence.md`.

### 3. Perform GO enrichment

Identify GO terms enriched among the neighbours of each query segment. Neighbours can be selected using:

- `knn`: nearest neighbours in embedding space (default).
- `BLAST`: top BLAST hits.
- `RANDOM`: randomly selected neighbours as a control.

The default neighbourhood size is 50.

```bash
python scripts/run_go_enrichment.py --config configs/go_config.yaml
```

**Required inputs:** An embedding file containing the query and background regions, GO ontology, and GO annotation table. The BLAST option additionally requires a BLAST output file.

**Output:** A CSV containing query identifiers, enriched GO terms with adjusted p-values, and term counts. Example columns are `query_id`, `term_adj_p`, and `term_counts`.

The related script `scripts/run_enrich_eval.py` evaluates or summarizes enrichment results. =

**Detailed documentation:** `docs/go-analysis.md`.

### 4. Train IDR-LM (optional)

Training code and configuration files are located in `src/idr_diverge/IDR_LM_train/`.

- `bert_config.json`: model architecture configuration.
- `idrlm_pretrain.yaml`: training arguments and file paths.
- `idrlm_train.py`: training script.
- `idrlm_embed.py`: embedding generation from trained or randomly initialized weights.

Activate `lm_train`, then configure the training FASTA, model configuration, optional resume checkpoint, and checkpoint output directories in `idrlm_pretrain.yaml`. Training configuration paths are resolved relative to the YAML file.

**Training data:** MobiDB-derived IDR sequences. [Add the exact dataset citation, release, and Zenodo download link.]

**Logging:** Training is configured to log to Weights & Biases. Configure the account, project, and run name, or disable that integration before running.

**Outputs:** Model checkpoints and training logs. If `load_best_model_at_end=True`, the final saved model uses the best checkpoint according to the selected evaluation metric.

**Detailed documentation:** `docs/training.md`.

## Outputs

| Analysis | Output |
| --- | --- |
| Embedding generation | HDF5 files containing sequence identifiers and embeddings. |
| Neighbour distance | `.pkl` dictionaries; structure depends on `dist_type` and `return_mode`. |
| FND | CSV containing group identifiers, FND values, and statistical results. |
| GO enrichment | CSV containing enriched GO terms, adjusted p-values, and term counts per query. |
| IDR-LM training | Model checkpoints and training logs. |

Output paths are specified in the workflow configurations. Full output schemas and examples belong in the corresponding workflow documentation.

> [!WARNING] > This repository is no longer maintained. Please check out [BioEmu2](https://github.com/microsoft/bioemu2).

[![DOI:10.1101/2024.12.05.626885](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.1101/2024.12.05.626885.svg)](https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.12.05.626885) [![Requires Python 3.10+](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.10+-blue.svg?logo=python&logoColor=white)](https://python.org/downloads) # Biomolecular Emulator (BioEmu) Biomolecular Emulator (BioEmu for short) is a model that samples from the approximated equilibrium distribution of structures for a protein monomer, given its amino acid sequence. For more information see our paper, [citation below](#citation). This repository contains inference code and model weights. ## Table of Contents - [Installation](#installation) - [Sampling structures](#sampling-structures) - [Steering to avoid chain breaks and clashes](#steering-to-avoid-chain-breaks-and-clashes) - [Azure AI Foundry](#azure-ai-foundry) - [Training data](#training-data) - [Get in touch](#get-in-touch) - [Citation](#citation) ## Installation bioemu is provided as a Linux-only pip-installable package. We support Python 3.10 and above: ```bash pip install bioemu ``` To install with CUDA support: ```bash pip install bioemu[cuda] ``` > [!NOTE] > BioEmu uses an inlined version of [ColabFold](https://github.com/sokrypton/ColabFold) and [AlphaFold2](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold) for MSA retrieval and embedding generation. These are bundled with the package — no separate environment or installation is needed. On first use, AlphaFold2 model weights (~3.5 GB) will be automatically downloaded to `~/.cache/colabfold/`. ## Sampling structures You can sample structures for a given protein sequence using the `sample` module. To run a tiny test using the default model parameters and denoising settings: ``` python -m bioemu.sample --sequence GYDPETGTWG --num_samples 10 --output_dir ~/test-chignolin ``` Alternatively, you can use the Python API: ```python from bioemu.sample import main as sample sample(sequence='GYDPETGTWG', num_samples=10, output_dir='~/test_chignolin') ``` The model parameters will be automatically downloaded from [huggingface](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/bioemu). A path to a single-sequence FASTA file can also be passed to the `sequence` argument. Sampling times will depend on sequence length and available infrastructure. The following table gives times for collecting 1000 samples measured on an A100 GPU with 80 GB VRAM for sequences of different lengths (using a `batch_size_100=20` setting in `sample.py`): | sequence length | time / min | | --------------: | ---------: | | 100 | 4 | | 300 | 40 | | 600 | 150 | By default, unphysical structures (steric clashes or chain discontinuities) will be filtered out, so you will typically get fewer samples in the output than requested. The difference can be very large if your protein has large disordered regions which are very likely to produce clashes. If you want to get all generated samples in the output, irrespective of whether they are physically valid, use the `--filter_samples=False` argument. > [!NOTE] > If you wish to use your own generated MSA instead of the ones retrieved via the ColabFold MMseqs2 server, you can pass an A3M file containing the query sequence as the first row to the `sequence` argument. Additionally, the `msa_host_url` argument can be used to override the default MSA query server. See [sample.py](./src/bioemu/sample.py) for more options. This code only supports sampling structures of monomers. You can try to sample multimers using the [linker trick](https://x.com/ag_smith/status/1417063635000598528), but in our limited experiments, this has not worked well. ## Steering to avoid chain breaks and clashes BioEmu includes a [steering system](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.06848) that guides the diffusion process toward more physically plausible protein structures. Steering applies potential energy functions during denoising to favor conformations that satisfy physical constraints. Two steering algorithms are available: - **SMC (Sequential Monte Carlo)**: Simulates multiple *candidate samples* (particles) per desired output sample, where the candidates are denoised in an unbiased way, and resamples between them according to the favorability of the provided potentials. This is the default for physical steering. - **FKC (Feynman–Kac Corrector)**: Uses importance weighting and may perform ESS-based resampling between particles; useful when targeting a specific collective variable value (e.g., RMSD to a reference). The samples are denoised with bias from the bias potential (reward). Empirically, using three (or up to 10) steering particles per output sample greatly reduces the number of unphysical samples (steric clashes or chain breaks) produced by the model. ### Quick start with steering Steering is configured via a single YAML file passed as `denoiser_config`. This file specifies the denoiser, potentials, and steering parameters together. Enable steering with physical constraints using the CLI: ```bash python -m bioemu.sample \ --sequence GYDPETGTWG \ --num_samples 100 \ --output_dir ~/steered-samples \ --denoiser_config src/bioemu/config/steering/physical_steering.yaml ``` Or using the Python API: ```python from bioemu.sample import main as sample sample( sequence='GYDPETGTWG', num_samples=100, output_dir='~/steered-samples', denoiser_config="src/bioemu/config/steering/physical_steering.yaml", ) ``` ### Key steering parameters Inside the steering YAML config (e.g., [`physical_steering.yaml`](./src/bioemu/config/steering/physical_steering.yaml)): - `num_particles`: Number of particles per sample (higher = stronger steering, more compute) - `ess_threshold`: Effective sample size threshold for resampling (0.0–1.0) - `start`: Diffusion time to start steering (0.0–1.0, default: 0.1; reverse process goes 1→0) - `end`: Diffusion time to stop steering (0.0–1.0, default: 0.0) - `fk_potentials`: List of potential energy functions to apply (Hydra-instantiated) ### Available potentials The [`physical_steering.yaml`](./src/bioemu/config/steering/physical_steering.yaml) configuration provides potentials for physical realism: - **CaCaDistance** + **UmbrellaPotential**: Prevents backbone discontinuities by penalizing large Cα–Cα distances - **PairwiseClash** + **UmbrellaPotential**: Avoids steric clashes between non-neighboring residues For custom steering, you can write your own YAML config targeting any combination of potentials and collective variables. See [`cv_steer.yaml`](./src/bioemu/config/steering/cv_steer.yaml) for an example that steers toward a target RMSD value using FKC. ## Azure AI Foundry BioEmu is also available on [Azure AI Foundry](https://ai.azure.com/). See [How to run BioEmu on Azure AI Foundry](AZURE_AI_FOUNDRY.md) for more details. ## Training data The molecular dynamics training data used for BioEmu is available on Zenodo: - [CATH](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15629740) - [Octapeptides](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15641199) - [MegaSim](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15641184) For a full description of these, see the paper. ## Reproducing results from the paper You can use this code together with code from [bioemu-benchmarks](https://github.com/microsoft/bioemu-benchmarks) to approximately reproduce results from our [paper]. - The `bioemu-v1.0` checkpoint contains the model weights used to produce the results in the preprint. Due to simplifications made in the embedding computation and a more efficient sampler, the results obtained with this code are not identical but consistent with the preprint statistics, i.e., mode coverage and free energy errors averaged over the proteins in a test set. Results for individual proteins may differ. - [Default] The `bioemu-v1.1` checkpoint contains the model weights used to produce the results in the published Science [paper]. - The `bioemu-v1.2` checkpoint contains the model weights trained from an extended set of MD simulations and experimental measurements of folding free energies. For more details, please check the [BIOEMU_RESULTS.md](https://github.com/microsoft/bioemu-benchmarks/blob/main/bioemu_benchmarks/BIOEMU_RESULTS.md) document on the bioemu-benchmarks repository. To use a specific checkpoint, you can specify the `model_name` in the `bioemu.sample` args, for example, `--model_name="bioemu-v1.1"`. ## Side-chain reconstruction and MD-relaxation BioEmu outputs structures in backbone frame representation. To reconstruct the side-chains, several tools are available. As an example, we interface with [HPacker](https://github.com/gvisani/hpacker) to conduct side-chain reconstruction, and also provide basic tooling for running a short molecular dynamics (MD) equilibration. > [!WARNING] > Side-chain reconstruction relies on [HPacker](https://github.com/gvisani/hpacker) which requires a [conda-based package manager](https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/latest/user-guide/install/index.html). Make sure that `conda` is in your `PATH` and that you have CUDA12-compatible drivers before running the following code. Note that `conda` is **not** required for BioEmu's core sampling functionality. Install optional dependencies: ```bash pip install bioemu[md] ``` You can compute side-chain reconstructions via the `bioemu.sidechains_relax` module: ```bash python -m bioemu.sidechain_relax --pdb-path path/to/topology.pdb --xtc-path path/to/samples.xtc ``` > [!NOTE] > The first time this module is invoked, it will attempt to install `hpacker` and its dependencies into a separate virtualenv using a bundled setup script. If the automatic setup fails, you can install hpacker manually by following the instructions at [hpacker's repository](https://github.com/gvisani/hpacker) and setting the `HPACKER_PYTHONBIN` environment variable to the path of the python executable where hpacker is installed. By default, side-chain reconstruction and local energy minimization are performed (no full MD integration for efficiency reasons). Note that the runtime of this code scales with the size of the system. We suggest running this code on a selection of samples rather than the full set. There are two other options: - To only run side-chain reconstruction without MD equilibration, add `--no-md-equil`. - To run a short NVT equilibration (0.1 ns), add `--md-protocol nvt_equil` To see the full list of options, call `python -m bioemu.sidechain_relax --help`. The script saves reconstructed all-heavy-atom structures in `samples_sidechain_rec.{pdb,xtc}` and MD-equilibrated structures in `samples_md_equil.{pdb,xtc}` (filename to be altered with `--outname other_name`). ## Third-party code - The code in `src/bioemu/openfold/` is copied from [OpenFold](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold) (Apache 2.0) with minor modifications described in the relevant source files. - The code in `src/_vendor/alphafold/` is a vendored, patched subset of [AlphaFold2](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold) v2.3.2 (Apache 2.0). See [src/_vendor/alphafold/README.md](src/_vendor/alphafold/README.md) for details on the modifications. - The code in `src/bioemu/colabfold_inline/` contains functions derived from [ColabFold](https://github.com/sokrypton/ColabFold) v1.5.4 (MIT). See the license headers in each file for details. ## Get in touch If you have any questions not covered here, please create an issue or contact the BioEmu team by writing to the corresponding author on our [paper]. ## Citation If you are using our code or model, please cite the following paper: ```bibtex @article{bioemu2025, title={Scalable emulation of protein equilibrium ensembles with generative deep learning}, author={Lewis, Sarah and Hempel, Tim and Jim{\'e}nez-Luna, Jos{\'e} and Gastegger, Michael and Xie, Yu and Foong, Andrew YK and Satorras, Victor Garc{\'\i}a and Abdin, Osama and Veeling, Bastiaan S and Zaporozhets, Iryna and Chen, Yaoyi and Yang, Soojung and Foster, Adam E. and Schneuing, Arne and Nigam, Jigyasa and Barbero, Federico and Stimper Vincent and Campbell, Andrew and Yim, Jason and Lienen, Marten and Shi, Yu and Zheng, Shuxin and Schulz, Hannes and Munir, Usman and Sordillo, Roberto and Tomioka, Ryota and Clementi, Cecilia and No{\'e}, Frank}, journal={Science}, pages={eadv9817}, year={2025}, publisher={American Association for the Advancement of Science}, doi={10.1126/science.adv9817} } ``` [paper]: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adv9817

## 是什么
Molly.jl 是一个纯 Julia 实现的分子动力学（MD）模拟包，用于模拟从惰性气体到生物大分子的物理系统。它提供力场、积分器、恒温器、恒压器、邻居列表、能量最小化、副本交换、蒙特卡洛模拟等功能，并支持 GPU 加速和可微分子模拟。

## 亮点
- **纯 Julia 实现**：无需外部依赖，易于安装和扩展。
- **可微分子模拟**：这是该包的独特功能，允许通过自动微分计算能量和力的梯度，用于力场优化和参数拟合。
- **模块化设计**：支持自定义相互作用、模拟器、恒温器、日志器等，便于用户扩展。
- **多后端 GPU 支持**：通过 KernelAbstractions.jl 支持 CUDA 等后端，实现自动多线程和 GPU 加速。
- **丰富的力场和相互作用**：包括 Lennard-Jones、Coulomb、Ewald/PME、键合相互作用、隐式溶剂 GBMV 等。
- **与外部工具兼容**：可读取 OpenMM 力场文件，通过 Chemfiles.jl 支持多种坐标和轨迹格式，并可调用 Python ASE 计算器。

## 为何对本课题有用
Molly.jl 直接适用于 IDR/IDP 的分子动力学模拟，尤其是其可微模拟特性可用于开发针对无序蛋白的力场（如论文中所述）。对于 IDR/IDP 的构象系综采样，Molly.jl 提供了副本交换、蒙特卡洛模拟和多种积分器，有助于探索无序蛋白的构象空间。此外，其模块化设计允许集成机器学习势（如 ANI），可用于构建无序蛋白的语言模型或混合 AI/物理模拟。对于 LLPS 研究，Molly.jl 支持多组分模拟和隐式溶剂模型，可模拟相分离行为。

## 怎么用
- **安装**：需要 Julia v1.10+，在 Julia REPL 中按 `]` 进入包模式，运行 `add Molly`。GPU 支持需额外安装如 `CUDA` 包。
- **主入口**：使用 `simulate!` 函数进行模拟，示例见 README 中的 Lennard-Jones 流体和蛋白质模拟。
- **输入数据**：支持通过 Chemfiles.jl 读取 PDB、DCD、XTC 等格式，力场文件为 OpenMM XML 格式。
- **输出数据**：可写入 DCD、XTC 等轨迹文件，并支持日志记录任意属性。
- **GPU 加速**：通过设置 `array_type=CuArray` 使用 GPU，但性能目前比 OpenMM 慢约 5 倍。
- **测试与示例**：`test/` 目录包含大量单元测试，`exercises/` 有 Jupyter notebook 教程，`scripts/` 有高级示例（如 AWH、TSS）。

## 核心 idea
Molly.jl 的核心创新在于将分子动力学模拟与自动微分结合，使得模拟过程可微，从而能够通过梯度下降优化力场参数或学习势能函数。这种可微模拟框架为无序蛋白的力场开发提供了新范式，能够直接利用实验数据或机器学习目标进行参数化。

## 可搬移点
- **可微模拟模块**：`src/` 中的力计算和积分器支持自动微分，可提取用于自定义的力场优化 Pipeline。
- **邻居列表实现**：`src/neighbors.jl` 中的邻居搜索算法（包括 CellListMap.jl 接口）可独立用于加速非键相互作用计算。
- **力场解析器**：`src/force_field.jl` 可读取 OpenMM XML 力场，可复用为其他模拟包的力场转换工具。
- **副本交换和蒙特卡洛模块**：`src/free_energy/` 中的副本交换和 TSS 方法可用于构象系综采样。
- **License**：MIT 许可，允许自由使用和修改，但需确认具体版本。
readme:
![Molly logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/master/docs/src/images/logo_molly.svg)

[![Build status](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/workflows/CI/badge.svg)](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/actions)
[![Coverage status](https://codecov.io/gh/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/branch/master/graph/badge.svg?token=RD9XF0W90L)](https://codecov.io/gh/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl)
[![Latest release](https://img.shields.io/github/release/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl.svg)](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/releases/latest)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green.svg)](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/blob/master/LICENSE.md)
[![Documentation stable](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-stable-blue.svg)](https://JuliaMolSim.github.io/Molly.jl/stable)
[![Documentation dev](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-dev-blue.svg)](https://JuliaMolSim.github.io/Molly.jl/dev)

Much of science can be explained by the movement and interaction of molecules.
Molecular dynamics (MD) is a computational technique used to explore these phenomena, from noble gases to biological macromolecules.
Molly.jl is a pure Julia package for MD, and for the simulation of physical systems more broadly.

The package is described in [a talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XTE5HSo-jx8) at JuliaCon 2024, [an earlier talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6G97jDVPlYc) at Enzyme Conference 2023 and [a tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rVRWIxLyjgE) at the MolSSI JuliaMolSim Workshop 2024.
[Slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1CvGwFn0XjiIfAQ562RlIPGjXRKnsNXLYjmPRDFS7SQs/edit?usp=sharing) are also available for a tutorial in 2025.

Implemented features include:
- Non-bonded interactions - Lennard-Jones van der Waals/repulsion force, electrostatic Coulomb potential and reaction field, gravitational potential, soft sphere potential, Mie potential, Buckingham potential, soft core variants for alchemical simulation.
- Bonded interactions - harmonic and Morse bonds, bond angles, torsion angles, harmonic position restraints, FENE bonds.
- Ewald and particle mesh Ewald (PME) electrostatic summation.
- Interface to allow definition of new interactions, simulators, thermostats, loggers etc.
- Read in OpenMM force field files and coordinate files supported by [Chemfiles.jl](https://github.com/chemfiles/Chemfiles.jl).
- Write out trajectory files in formats supported by Chemfiles.jl, including DCD and XTC.
- Verlet, velocity Verlet, Störmer-Verlet, flexible Langevin, Nosé-Hoover and multiple time stepping integrators.
- Andersen, Berendsen and velocity rescaling thermostats.
- C-rescale, Monte Carlo and Berendsen barostats with flexible virial calculation.
- Steepest descent, FIRE and L-BFGS energy minimization.
- Replica exchange molecular dynamics.
- Monte Carlo simulation.
- Periodic, triclinic and infinite boundary conditions.
- Constraints with SHAKE and RATTLE.
- Virtual sites.
- Flexible loggers to track arbitrary properties throughout simulations.
- Cutoff and mixing algorithms for non-bonded interactions.
- Various neighbor list implementations to speed up the calculation of non-bonded forces, including the use of [CellListMap.jl](https://github.com/m3g/CellListMap.jl).
- Implicit solvent GBSA methods.
- [Unitful.jl](https://github.com/PainterQubits/Unitful.jl) compatibility so numbers have physical meaning.
- Set up crystal systems using [SimpleCrystals.jl](https://github.com/ejmeitz/SimpleCrystals.jl).
- Flexible bias potentials and collective variables.
- Native support for the [ANI](https://github.com/aiqm/torchani) machine learning interatomic potential.
- Automatic multithreading.
- GPU acceleration on all backends supported by [KernelAbstractions.jl](https://github.com/JuliaGPU/KernelAbstractions.jl), with better performance on CUDA-enabled devices.
- Run with Float64, Float32 or other float types.
- Some analysis functions, e.g. RDF.
- Visualise simulations as animations with [Makie.jl](https://makie.juliaplots.org/stable).
- Compatibility with [AtomsBase.jl](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/AtomsBase.jl) and [AtomsCalculators.jl](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/AtomsCalculators.jl).
- Interface to use Python [ASE](https://ase-lib.org) calculators.
- Control of random numbers during simulation, allowing reproducible stochastic simulations.
- Differentiable molecular simulation. This is a unique feature of the package and the focus of its current development.

Features not yet implemented include:
- Optimal GPU performance - currently we are ~5x slower than OpenMM on CUDA GPUs.
- Protein preparation - solvent box, add hydrogens etc.
- Simulators such as metadynamics.
- Quantum mechanical modelling.
- Domain decomposition algorithms.

## Installation

[Julia](https://julialang.org/downloads) is required, with Julia v1.10 or later required to get the latest version of Molly.
It is recommended to run on the current stable Julia release for the best performance.
Install Molly from the Julia REPL.
Enter the package mode by pressing `]` and run `add Molly`.
If you want to run on a GPU you will also need to install the appropriate package for your system, e.g. `add CUDA`.

## Usage

Some examples are given here, see [the documentation](https://juliamolsim.github.io/Molly.jl/stable/documentation) for more on how to use the package.

Simulation of a Lennard-Jones fluid:
```julia
using Molly

n_atoms = 100
boundary = CubicBoundary(2.0u"nm")
temp = 298.0u"K"
atom_mass = 10.0u"g/mol"

atoms = [Atom(mass=atom_mass, σ=0.3u"nm", ϵ=0.2u"kJ * mol^-1") for i in 1:n_atoms]
coords = place_atoms(n_atoms, boundary; min_dist=0.3u"nm")
velocities = [random_velocity(atom_mass, temp) for i in 1:n_atoms]
pairwise_inters = (LennardJones(use_neighbors=false),)

simulator = VelocityVerlet(
    dt=0.002u"ps",
    coupling=AndersenThermostat(temp, 1.0u"ps"),
)

sys = System(
    atoms=atoms,
    coords=coords,
    boundary=boundary,
    velocities=velocities,
    pairwise_inters=pairwise_inters,
    loggers=(temp=TemperatureLogger(100),),
)

simulate!(sys, simulator, 10_000)
```

Simulation of a protein on GPU:
```julia
using Molly, CUDA

data_dir = joinpath(dirname(pathof(Molly)), "..", "data")
T = Float32
ff = MolecularForceField(
    T,
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "ff99SBildn.xml"),
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "tip3p_standard.xml"),
)

sys = System(
    joinpath(data_dir, "6mrr_equil.pdb"),
    ff;
    nonbonded_method=:pme,
    loggers=(
        energy=TotalEnergyLogger(10),
        writer=TrajectoryWriter(10, "traj_6mrr_5ps.dcd"),
    ),
    array_type=CuArray,
)

minimizer = SteepestDescentMinimizer()
simulate!(sys, minimizer)

temp = T(298.0)u"K"
random_velocities!(sys, temp)
simulator = Langevin(
    dt=T(0.001)u"ps",
    temperature=temp,
    friction=T(1.0)u"ps^-1",
    coupling=MonteCarloBarostat(T(1.0)u"bar", temp, sys.boundary),
)

simulate!(sys, simulator, 5_000)
```
The above 5 ps simulation looks something like this when you view it in PyMOL:
![MD simulation](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/raw/master/docs/src/images/sim_6mrr.gif)

## Contributing

Contributions are very welcome including reporting bugs, fixing bugs, adding new features, improving performance, adding tests and improving documentation.
Feel free to open an issue or use the channels below to discuss your contribution.
New features will generally require tests to be added as well.
As described in the documentation, potentials implementing the [AtomsCalculators](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/AtomsCalculators.jl) interface can be used with Molly.
If you have an interesting example of such a potential in your package, do contribute an example to the Molly documentation.
See the [roadmap issue](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/issues/2) for some discussion of recent progress and future plans.

## 是什么
BioEmu2 是微软研究院 AI for Science 团队开发的一个基础模型，用于生物分子结构与动力学模拟。它能够预测折叠结构、采样平衡构象系综，并通过隐式迁移算子模型沿时间轴传播结构。该系统支持包含蛋白质、核酸、配体及其他化学组分的分子体系，提供命令行和 Python API 两种使用方式。

## 亮点
- **多组分分子体系支持**：不仅支持蛋白质，还支持核酸、配体等，覆盖更广泛的生物分子场景。
- **平衡采样与结构预测一体化**：从命令行或 Python 即可完成平衡采样和结构预测，简化工作流。
- **时间传播能力**：通过隐式迁移算子模型生成时间滞后轨迹，实现结构随时间的演化。
- **接触条件与推理时引导**：支持接触条件约束和推理时引导，可向期望性质（如物理合理性）倾斜采样。
- **上下文并行采样**：支持跨多 GPU 的上下文并行，处理无法单卡容纳的大结构。
- **MSA 灵活控制**：可从 ColabFold 检索或本地加载 A3M 文件，支持 MSA 子采样和自定义 MSA 推理。
- **工程化完善**：提供 CLI、Python 函数式 API、示例脚本、单元测试，以及详细的文档和教程。

## 为何对本课题有用
BioEmu2 直接面向生物分子结构预测与构象系综采样，与 IDR/IDP 研究高度相关。其平衡采样能力可用于生成无序蛋白的构象系综，而时间传播功能可模拟 IDR 的动态行为。接触条件与推理时引导允许研究者针对特定性质（如无序倾向、结合界面）进行采样，这对于研究 IDR 介导的分子互作（如 LLPS 中的多价相互作用）尤为有价值。此外，其多组分支持（蛋白质-配体、蛋白质-核酸）可扩展到 IDR 与配体或核酸的互作建模。上下文并行技术则为大规模 IDR 体系（如相分离凝聚体）的模拟提供了计算可行性。

## 怎么用
- **安装**：需要 Linux 和 NVIDIA GPU（compute capability ≥7.0），Python 3.12-3.14。使用 `pip install ".[cuda]"` 或 `pip install ".[cuda12]"`（针对 V100 等旧 GPU）。依赖见 `pyproject.toml`，包括 torch、cuequivariance、openmm、rdkit 等。
- **主入口**：命令行工具 `bioemu2`，或 Python 导入 `from bioemu2 import EmuSession, System, load_model, save_frames`。
- **快速开始**：
  - 平衡采样：`bioemu2 sample-equilibrium --pdb-id 1AKE --out outputs/adk`
  - 结构预测：`bioemu2 predict-structure --pdb-id 1UBQ --num-samples 1 --out outputs/ubiq`
  - 时间传播：`bioemu2 propagate --x0-cif outputs/adk/topology.cif --x0-xtc outputs/adk/samples.xtc --lag-time-ns 1 --out outputs/adk-propagated`
- **输入/输出**：输入可为 PDB ID、结构文件或序列（通过 YAML 系统文件定义），输出为 `topology.cif` 和 `samples.xtc`（轨迹文件）。
- **示例与测试**：`examples/` 目录包含可运行的 Python 脚本（带 `# %%` 标记），如 `sample_structures.py`、`simulate_a_trajectory.py` 等；`tests/` 目录有单元测试，可用于调试。
- **GPU 需求**：必须使用 NVIDIA GPU，支持多 GPU 上下文并行（至少 4 卡）。

## 核心 idea
BioEmu2 的核心方法学在于将结构预测、平衡采样和时间传播统一在一个基础模型框架中，通过隐式迁移算子模型实现时间演化，从而无需显式分子动力学模拟即可生成动态轨迹。其创新点在于：利用扩散模型（从代码结构推测）进行构象生成，并通过接触条件与推理时引导实现目标性质约束，使得采样过程可调控、可偏向，从而在保持精度的同时大幅提升采样效率。

## 可搬移点
- **平衡采样模块**（`src/bioemu2/sampling.py` 及相关）：可解耦用于自定义构象系综生成，尤其适合 IDR 的 ensemble 采样。
- **时间传播模块**（`src/bioemu2/propagation.py`）：可移植用于 IDR 动态模拟，替代昂贵的 MD 模拟。
- **接触条件与引导机制**（`src/bioemu2/conditioning/`）：可借鉴其实现，用于在采样中施加 IDR 相关约束（如结合位点、无序倾向）。
- **上下文并行实现**（`src/bioemu2/context_parallel/`）：可迁移至大规模 IDR 体系模拟，解决显存瓶颈。
- **MSA 处理模块**（`src/bioemu2/msa/`）：可复用其 MSA 加载与子采样逻辑，用于 IDR 序列分析。
- **License**：MIT，允许自由使用和修改，但需注意第三方组件（见 NOTICES.md）的许可。

**注意**：以上可搬移点基于代码结构推测，具体函数接口需查阅源码确认。

# BioEmu2 ### A foundation model for biomolecular structure and dynamics **Predict folded structures, sample equilibrium ensembles, and propagate structures forward in time.** [Installation](#installation) · [Quick start](#quick-start) · [Tutorials](#tutorials) · [Documentation](docs/)
BioEmu2 simulating the PUMA BH3 peptide binding MCL-1.
--- BioEmu2, short for "biomolecular emulator", is developed by Microsoft Research AI for Science. Key features include: - molecular systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, and other chemical components; - equilibrium sampling and structure prediction from the command line or Python; - time-lagged trajectory generation with implicit transfer operator models; - contact conditioning and inference-time steering toward desired properties; - context-parallel sampling of structures that do not fit on one GPU. ## System requirements BioEmu2 requires Linux and an NVIDIA GPU; macOS and Windows are not supported. The `cuda` extra installs CUDA 13 cuEquivariance, which requires compute capability 7.5 or newer, such as NVIDIA T4, A100, RTX A6000, L40S, H100, and B200 ([CUDA 13 release notes](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.0.0/cuda-toolkit-release-notes/index.html#deprecated-architectures)). GPUs with compute capability 7.0 (Volta, such as NVIDIA V100) need the CUDA 12 [installation](#installation) instead. We have tested V100 (compute capability 7.0), T4 (7.5, with the CUDA 12 installation), A100 and RTX A6000 (8.0 and 8.6), and B200 (10.0); other eligible GPUs have not been verified end to end. Check your GPU's compute capability with `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,compute_cap --format=csv`. Context-parallel sampling requires at least four GPUs. ## Installation Use Python 3.12, 3.13, or 3.14 on a supported Linux machine. We recommend installing BioEmu2 in an isolated [virtual environment](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html) or [conda environment](https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/latest/user-guide/tasks/manage-environments.html). To install in an isolated virtual environment, create and activate it from the repository root: ```bash python3.12 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate ``` Replace `python3.12` with the name or path of your Python 3.12, 3.13, or 3.14 executable if needed. Use `python -m pip` so packages are installed into the active Python environment rather than a different interpreter's `pip`. Run the installation command for your GPU from the repository root. For GPUs with compute capability 7.5 or newer, such as NVIDIA T4, A100, RTX A6000, L40S, H100, and B200, use the `cuda` extra: ```bash python -m pip install ".[cuda]" ``` Compute capability 7.0 (Volta, such as NVIDIA V100) is the oldest supported; on these GPUs, use the `cuda12` extra with the PyTorch CUDA 12.6 package index: ```bash python -m pip install ".[cuda12]" \ --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126 ``` GPUs with compute capability below 7.0 are not supported. We tested BioEmu2 and evaluated its benchmark metrics with Python 3.12. Python 3.13 and 3.14 pass the test suite, but we have not evaluated benchmark metrics with them. For development, see [DEVELOPER.md](DEVELOPER.md). For Jupyter or VS Code notebooks, follow the [notebook quickstart](#notebook-quickstart) to install visualization dependencies and register a kernel. ## Quick start ### CLI Sample eight equilibrium conformations of adenylate kinase (PDB 1AKE): ```bash bioemu2 sample-equilibrium \ --pdb-id 1AKE \ --out outputs/adk ``` To sample a system that is not a PDB entry, pass a system YAML file with `--system` instead of `--pdb-id`. Start from one of the [example system YAML files](examples/README.md#example-system-yaml-files). Or predict a folded structure from a PDB entry: ```bash bioemu2 predict-structure \ --pdb-id 1UBQ \ --num-samples 1 \ --out outputs/ubiquitin ``` Propagate each sampled adenylate kinase conformation by 1 ns: ```bash bioemu2 propagate \ --x0-cif outputs/adk/topology.cif \ --x0-xtc outputs/adk/samples.xtc \ --lag-time-ns 1 \ --out outputs/adk-propagated ``` Run `bioemu2 --help` to list all commands. ### Python API using EmuSession Construct an `EmuSession` to sample and propagate structures: ```python from pathlib import Path from bioemu2 import EmuSession, System, load_model, save_frames model = load_model() # Predict a folded structure for ubiquitin. ubiquitin = System.from_pdb_id("1UBQ") prediction = EmuSession(ubiquitin, model=model, mode="structure").sample(num_samples=1) save_frames(prediction, Path("outputs/ubiquitin")) # Sample equilibrium conformations of adenylate kinase. adk = System.from_pdb_id("1AKE") emu = EmuSession(adk, model=model, mode="equilibrium") samples = emu.sample(num_samples=8) save_frames(samples, Path("outputs/adk")) # Propagate each adenylate kinase conformation by 1 ns. endpoints = emu.propagate(samples, lag_time_ns=1.0) save_frames(endpoints, Path("outputs/adk-propagated")) ``` `save_frames()` writes `samples.xtc` and `topology.cif` to each output directory. See [define molecular systems](docs/system.md), [predict and sample structures](docs/sampling.md), and [propagate structures](docs/propagation.md) for more options. The functional Python APIs provide [high-level sampling](docs/functional-api.md#sample-structures) and [propagation](docs/functional-api.md#propagate-structures) functions similar to the CLI commands, plus lower-level workflows for explicit control of embeddings and samplers. ## More workflows ### Steer sampling Choose a steering sampler to favour structures with desired properties: ```bash bioemu2 sample-equilibrium \ --system src/bioemu2/assets/examples/systems/myoglobin_101m.yaml \ --out outputs/myoglobin \ --sampler edm_gd ``` See [steer sampling](docs/steering.md) and [define steering potentials](docs/potentials.md) to select an algorithm and configure its objective. ### Sample large structures across multiple GPUs Context parallelism distributes the model's pair representations across a square mesh of GPUs, reducing the memory required on each device: ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 \ torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=4 \ --module bioemu2.cp sample-equilibrium \ --pdb-id 1AKE \ --checkpoint bioemu2-preview \ --num-samples 3 \ --out outputs/adk-cp ``` See [sample large structures with context parallelism](docs/context-parallel-sampling.md) for mesh requirements, the Python API, and current limitations. ### Inspect and subsample MSAs Retrieve an alignment from ColabFold or load your own A3M files, inspect the raw sequences, and select or randomly subsample rows with Python indexing. Pass the resulting `MSA` directly to `EmuSession` to control the alignment used for structure prediction, equilibrium sampling, or propagation without manually constructing embeddings. See [use multiple sequence alignments](docs/msa.md) for local-file loading, [MSA subsampling](docs/msa.md#select-rows-and-subsample-an-msa), and [custom-MSA inference](docs/msa.md#use-a-custom-msa-for-inference). ## Tutorials - [Define molecular systems](docs/system.md) from PDB IDs, structure files, or sequences. - [Convert Boltz input YAML](docs/boltz.md) into systems you can sample from. - [Customise multiple-sequence alignments](docs/msa.md) used to condition sampling. - [Predict and sample structures](docs/sampling.md) for a system. - [Improve sampling speed and scale to bigger systems](docs/speed-and-capacity.md) by choosing batch size and precision. - [Load a model checkpoint](docs/checkpoints.md), choose where checkpoints are cached, or use a local checkpoint. - [Propagate structures through time](docs/propagation.md). - [Reuse trunk embeddings](docs/reuse-embeddings.md) across sampling and propagation calls, in memory or on disk. - [Use the functional Python API](docs/functional-api.md) to sample and propagate without an `EmuSession`. - [Steer sampling](docs/steering.md) towards structures with desired properties. - [Define steering potentials](docs/potentials.md) that encode the properties you want to favour. - [Sample large structures](docs/context-parallel-sampling.md) across multiple GPUs with context parallelism. ## Notebook quickstart The [`examples`](examples) directory contains complete workflows as regular Python files split into executable cells with `# %%` markers. This Python Interactive format provides notebook-style cells while keeping the examples as plain `.py` files. They require a Linux machine with a supported NVIDIA GPU and network access. Activate a Python environment as described in [installation](#installation). From the repository root, install BioEmu2 with the visualization dependencies and register a kernel. The `viz` extra includes `ipykernel` and `py3Dmol`: ```bash python -m pip install ".[cuda,viz]" python -m ipykernel install --user --name bioemu2 --display-name "BioEmu2" ``` On compute capability 7.0 GPUs, such as NVIDIA V100, replace the first command with: ```bash python -m pip install ".[cuda12,viz]" \ --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126 ``` Select the **BioEmu2** kernel in Jupyter or VS Code. If registration succeeds but the kernel does not appear in VS Code, restart VS Code and try again. To check that it uses the environment you installed into, run `import sys; print(sys.executable)` in a cell. The examples load system YAML from the installed `bioemu2` package, regardless of the working directory. Relative `outputs/` paths are written under the current working directory. Open a single-GPU example in VS Code and select **Run Cell**, or run **Jupyter: Run Current File in Interactive Window** from the Command Palette. Launch the context-parallel example with `torchrun` as described in the [context-parallel sampling guide](docs/context-parallel-sampling.md#python-api). The `# %%` markers are ordinary Python comments, so you can also run a single-GPU example as a regular script, for example `python examples/sample_structures.py`. The script computes the same results and writes the same output files as running the cells interactively. 3D structure views are not displayed. Matplotlib plots open in separate windows if a graphical display is available, and the script continues after you close them. To run the cells interactively without VS Code, convert an example to a Jupyter notebook with [Jupytext](https://jupytext.readthedocs.io/) and open it in JupyterLab: ```bash python -m pip install jupytext jupyterlab jupytext --to notebook examples/sample_structures.py jupyter lab examples/sample_structures.ipynb ``` Select the **BioEmu2** kernel, then run individual cells or choose **Run All Cells** from the **Run** menu. In VS Code, you can instead run **Jupyter: Export Current Python File as Jupyter Notebook** from the Command Palette. Generated `.ipynb` files are ignored by Git. ## License BioEmu2 is released under the [MIT License](LICENSE). It includes code and reference data adapted from other open-source projects; the [third-party notices](NOTICES.md) identify those components and their licenses.

one_liner: PARROT 是一个基于循环神经网络的通用蛋白质序列-残基属性预测工具，虽非专为 IDP/IDR 互作设计，但其序列级预测框架可迁移用于无序蛋白互作相关属性建模。
card:
## 是什么
PARROT 是一个基于双向循环神经网络（BRNN）的蛋白质序列分析工具，提供命令行接口，支持用户自定义的序列-标签映射数据进行训练和预测。它适用于多种蛋白质生物信息学任务，包括回归和分类问题，以及序列级和残基级的数据。

## 亮点
- **易用性**：通过简单的命令行接口（`parrot-train`、`parrot-optimize`、`parrot-predict`）即可完成训练、超参数优化和预测，无需深入编程。
- **灵活性**：支持回归和分类，以及序列级和残基级标签，适应多种任务。
- **自动超参数优化**：内置贝叶斯优化（`parrot-optimize`）自动搜索学习率、隐藏层数和隐藏向量大小，提升模型性能。
- **可扩展性**：基于 PyTorch 实现，易于修改和扩展，且提供 Python 包安装和源码克隆两种方式。

## 为何对本课题有用
PARROT 直接适用于 IDR/IDP 相关的序列-功能预测任务，例如预测无序区域、结合位点或相分离倾向性。其序列到标签的映射框架可以轻松适配 IDR 的残基级属性预测（如无序倾向、相互作用热点），且支持自定义训练数据，便于整合实验或模拟数据。此外，其 BRNN 架构可迁移至无序蛋白语言模型的构建，或作为基线模型与更复杂的架构（如 Transformer）对比。

## 怎么用
- **安装**：`pip install idptools-parrot` 或克隆仓库后 `pip install .`。依赖见 `pyproject.toml`，核心依赖包括 numpy、scipy、torch、scikit-learn 等。
- **主命令**：
  - `parrot-train`：训练网络，需提供数据文件（TSV 格式，每行：seqID 序列 标签1 标签2 ...）。
  - `parrot-optimize`：超参数优化，需安装 `[optimize]` 扩展。
  - `parrot-predict`：用训练好的模型预测新序列。
- **数据格式**：输入为 TSV 文件，序列和标签以空格分隔；序列级数据每行三列，残基级数据每行序列长度+2列。
- **示例**：`data/` 目录提供示例数据集，`tests/` 目录包含单元测试，可用于调试。
- **GPU**：需要 GPU 加速以提升训练速度，但 CPU 也可运行。

## 核心 idea
PARROT 的核心在于将蛋白质序列编码为数值特征，通过双向循环神经网络捕捉序列上下文信息，从而学习序列到标签的映射。其创新点在于提供了一个通用、易用的框架，使用户无需深入了解深度学习即可训练高性能模型，同时通过贝叶斯优化自动调整关键超参数，确保模型在不同数据集上的适应性。

## 可搬移点
- **序列编码模块**（`parrot/encode_sequence.py`）：可将氨基酸序列转换为数值向量，可独立用于其他模型。
- **BRNN 架构**（`parrot/brnn_architecture.py`）：可复用的双向 RNN 模型，可替换为其他序列模型。
- **数据处理流程**（`parrot/process_input_data.py`）：处理 TSV 输入，支持序列级和残基级标签，可移植到自定义 Pipeline。
- **贝叶斯优化**（`parrot/bayesian_optimization.py`）：超参数搜索逻辑可复用。
- **许可证**：MIT 许可证，允许自由使用和修改，但需确认具体条款。

# PARROT: Protein Analysis using RecuRrent neural networks On Training data

**PARROT** encodes a computationally-robust bidirectional recurrent neural network (BRNN) behind an easy-to-use commandline interface. PARROT is well-suited for a variety of protein bioinformatics tasks. With only an input data file containing sequences and mapped values, the user can automatically train a network for whatever purpose. This trained network can then be applied to new, unlabeled data to generate predictions and generate biological hypotheses.

This package can handle regression and classification ML problems, as well as sequence-mapped and residue-mapped input data.

#### Version 1.7.6 [Ma 2025]
## Installation:

PARROT is available through GitHub or the Python Package Index (PyPI). To install the base version of PARROT through PyPI, run

	$ pip install idptools-parrot

It is possible that you may experience errors depending on what Python packages are already installed on your machine. If you encounter this, try installing PARROT in a "clean" virtual environment using conda:

	$ conda create --name <env_name> python=3.9
	$ conda activate <env_name>

Then install PARROT with pip.

Alternatively, to clone the GitHub repository and gain the ability to modify a local copy of the code, run:

	$ git clone https://github.com/idptools/parrot.git
	$ cd parrot
	$ pip install .

This will install PARROT locally. If you modify the source code in the local repository, be sure to reinstall with pip.

**JULY 2022 UPDATE**

To mitigate package version dependency issues involving Python, GPy, and PyTorch, new releases of PARROT have separated 
`parrot-optimize` as an optional add-on installation. All of the documentation for using `parrot-optimize` is unchanged.
However, if you wish to use the hyperparameter optimization, there are now slight differences in how you install PARROT.

To install the PARROT that is compatible with `parrot-optimize` install via pip using:

	$ pip install idptools-parrot[optimize]

or

	$ pip install "idptools-parrot[optimize]"

Alternatively if you have the PARROT repository cloned locally you can install using

	$ pip install ".[optimize]"


## Usage:

For detailed information on installation and examples, please visit the [documentation pages](https://idptools-parrot.readthedocs.io/en/latest/).

There are three primary commands that can be run within the parrot package:

1. Train a network with user-specified hyperparameters
2. Train a network with automatically-determined, optimal hyperparameters
3. Generate predictions on unlabeled sequences using a trained network

### Input data format:

Before data can be integrated into training a PARROT network, it must be formatted in the following manner:

	seqID1 seq1 seq1data1 <seq1data2> <seq1data3> ... <seq1dataN1>  
	seqID2 seq2 seq2data1 <seq2data2> <seq2data3> ... <seq2dataN2>  
	.
	.
	.  
	seqIDM seqM seqMdata1 <seqMdata2> <seqMdata3> ... <seqMdataNM>
  
Where Ni is the length of sequence i, and M is the total number of labeled sequences. Items must be whitespace-separated.
For **sequence-mapped data** (i.e. each sequence constitutes a *single datapoint*), each row will only contain three columns.

Note that it is not required that sequences are the same length. For example, if Sequence #1 has 12 amino acids and Sequence #2 has 15 amino acids, these two rows in the input file will contain 14 and 17 fields, respectively.

Optionally, you may use datasets that exclude the first column containing the ID of each sequence. In this case, be sure to use the `--excludeSeqID` flag.

**Classification problem:** the labeled data should be integer class labels. For example, if there are 3 classes, then each datapoint should be either a '0', '1', or '2' (with no quotation marks).
  
**Regression problem:** If the user wishes to map each sequence or residue to a continuous real number, then each datapoint should be a float

For example, datasets, see the TSV files provided in the **/data** folder.

### 1. Train a network with provided hyperparameters: ``parrot-train``

The ``parrot-train`` command is the primary command for training a network with PARROT. By default, users need only to specify their data, where they want to save their output, and some basic information on the type of machine learning problem they are tackling. Beyond this, there are a suite of other options that users can provide to tailor their network to their particular needs. Users can provide specific hyperparameters to craft their network, they can manually specify what samples in their data set are trained on and which are held out as test data, they can choose to output information and figures on their network's performance on the test data, and much more!

### 2. Optimize hyperparameters and train a network: ``parrot-optimize``

The ``parrot-optimize`` command initiates an extensive search for the best-performing network hyperparameters for a given dataset using Bayesian optimization. Three hyperparameters, the learning rate, the number of hidden layers, and hidden vector size can greatly impact network performance and training speed, so it is important to tune these for each particular dataset. This command will search across hyperparameter space by iteratively training and validating network performance (with 5-fold cross-validation). The best-performing hyperparameters will be selected and used to train a network from scratch as if running ``parrot_train`` with these parameters. Note that since this command takes a significant amount of time to run since it involvessearching for the best hyperparameters.

### 3. Generate predictions with a trained network: ``parrot-predict``

Once a network has been trained for a particular machine learning task, the user can generate predictions on new sequences with this network using the ``parrot-predict`` command. The user provides a list of sequences they would like to predict and the saved network, and a file is outputted with the predictions.

one_liner: 该仓库是 Boltz-2 的 Colab 封装工具，提供生物分子结构预测与结合亲和力预测，虽非专门针对 IDP/IDR，但可迁移用于无序蛋白参与的分子互作建模。
card:
## 是什么

Boltz2-Notebook 是一个基于 Google Colab 的交互式前端，将 Boltz-2 扩散模型封装为引导式表单，用于生物分子（蛋白质、DNA、RNA 和小分子配体）的 3D 结构预测和结合亲和力预测。它无需安装、无需命令行，即可在浏览器中运行，同时支持在本地 Linux 机器上运行。

## 亮点

- **零门槛交互**：通过引导式表单和实时校验（序列、SMILES、CCD 代码），用户无需编写 YAML 或命令行即可配置复杂的生物分子系统。
- **自动化工作流**：从参数生成到引擎运行再到结果分析，全部自动化，并生成自包含的 HTML 报告（含图表、3D 查看器）。
- **健壮的工程实现**：包含安装脚本、环境变量控制、错误诊断（如 CUDA 内存不足的提示）、以及 `doctor` 命令用于调试。
- **多版本兼容**：支持 Python 3.10–3.13，针对不同运行时自动选择官方包或社区 fork。
- **批量处理能力**：Batch 笔记本支持从 CSV/FASTA 文件批量输入，并带有排序功能。

## 为何对本课题有用

- **IDR/IDP 结构预测**：Boltz-2 本身是扩散模型，可预测蛋白质结构，对 IDR 区域可能给出低 pLDDT 分数，这有助于识别无序区域。该笔记本提供了便捷的接口来运行此类预测。
- **分子互作建模**：支持多链复合物、配体、共价键、口袋约束等，可直接用于研究 IDR 与配体或其他蛋白的互作。
- **结合亲和力预测**：提供 IC50、pIC50 和 ΔG 估计，可用于评估 IDR 介导的互作强度。
- **可迁移的工程模式**：其“引导式表单 + 自动化脚本”模式可复用于构建其他计算工具的交互界面，降低使用门槛。

## 怎么用

- **主入口**：在 Colab 中打开 `Boltz2.ipynb`，选择 GPU 运行时（T4 或更好），依次运行单元格。
- **安装与依赖**：`pyproject.toml` 定义包依赖（numpy, pyyaml, biopython, pandas, matplotlib, requests），可选依赖包括 rdkit（配体）、py3Dmol（查看器）、boltz 引擎（需单独安装）。
- **输入格式**：通过表单输入序列（蛋白质/RNA/DNA）、SMILES 或 CCD 代码（配体），可上传 MSA（.a3m）或模板（PDB/MMCIF）。
- **输出格式**：预测结构（PDB/MMCIF）、置信度分数（pLDDT、PAE、pTM、ipTM）、结合亲和力（IC50、pIC50、ΔG）、HTML 报告。
- **调试**：运行 `python -m boltz2nb.doctor /content/boltz_data/<job>` 诊断问题。
- **本地运行**：克隆仓库，`pip install -e ".[ligand,viewer]" "boltz[cuda]==2.2.1"`，然后运行脚本。

## 核心 idea

核心方法学在于**将复杂的生物分子预测流程封装为可交互的、自包含的模块化脚本**，通过环境变量和配置文件解耦用户输入与引擎执行，使得非专家用户也能利用先进的扩散模型进行结构预测和亲和力评估。

## 可搬移点

- **YAML 构建器**（`boltz2nb/yaml_builder.py`）：可将用户输入转换为 Boltz 引擎所需的 YAML 配置，此逻辑可独立复用，用于自定义 Pipeline 中生成输入。
- **结果分析模块**（`boltz2nb/analysis.py`）：将置信度分数映射到残基、计算界面统计，可提取用于 IDR 区域的 pLDDT 分析。
- **批处理逻辑**（`boltz2nb/batch.py`）：支持 CSV/FASTA 批量输入，可复用于高通量筛选。
- **诊断工具**（`boltz2nb/doctor.py`）：检查输出文件一致性，可借鉴用于自定义 Pipeline 的验证。
- **License**: MIT，允许自由使用和修改，但需确认 Boltz-2 引擎的许可证（README 未说明）。
readme:
### Biomolecular structure and binding-affinity prediction with Boltz-2, in your browser [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/AtharvaTilewale/boltz2-notebook/blob/main/Boltz2.ipynb) [![bioRxiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/bioRxiv-10.64898%2F2026.09.18.752645-b31b1b)](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.18.752645) [![CI](https://github.com/AtharvaTilewale/boltz2-notebook/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/AtharvaTilewale/boltz2-notebook/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-5A6985)](LICENSE) ![Python 3.10 to 3.13](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.10%E2%80%933.13-3B4FD6?logo=python&logoColor=white) [Website](https://atharvatilewale.github.io/boltz2-notebook/) · [Guide](https://atharvatilewale.github.io/boltz2-notebook/docs/use-cases.html) · [FAQ](https://atharvatilewale.github.io/boltz2-notebook/docs/faq.html) · [Paper](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.18.752645) · [Report an issue](https://github.com/AtharvaTilewale/boltz2-notebook/issues)
--- **Boltz2-Notebook** puts [Boltz-2](https://github.com/jwohlwend/boltz) behind a guided form in Google Colab. Describe your molecules (proteins, DNA, RNA and small-molecule ligands), press run, and get a predicted 3-D structure with confidence scores, a binding-affinity estimate and a self-contained report. No installation, no command line, no YAML to write. The same code also runs on your own Linux machine. ## Quick start 1. **Open the [default notebook in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/AtharvaTilewale/boltz2-notebook/blob/main/Boltz2.ipynb)** and choose *Runtime ▸ Change runtime type ▸ T4 GPU*. 2. Run **Install** and **Download model weights**, once per session (about 6 GB of model files). 3. Run **Generate Parameters**, describe your system in the form and press **Save configuration**. 4. Run **Run Boltz2 Engine** (2 to 10 minutes on a T4), then **Analyse Results** for the plots, the 3-D viewer and the HTML report. ## Choose a notebook | Notebook | Use it for | Status | | |:--|:--|:--|:--| | **Advanced** (default) | Everything: proteins, DNA/RNA, ligands, templates, constraints, covalent bonds, modified residues, custom MSA | ![Stable](https://img.shields.io/badge/Stable-Default-green) | [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/AtharvaTilewale/boltz2-notebook/blob/main/Boltz2.ipynb) | | **Standard** | Proteins and small-molecule ligands, with a shorter form | ![Stable](https://img.shields.io/badge/Stable-Mature-green) | [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/AtharvaTilewale/boltz2-notebook/blob/main/colab/v1/Boltz2_v1.0.0.ipynb) | | **Batch** | Screening many inputs from a CSV or FASTA file, with ranking | ![Experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/Pre--release-Experimental-orange) | [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/AtharvaTilewale/boltz2-notebook/blob/main/batch/Boltz2_Batch_v1_beta.ipynb) | Not sure? Start with **Advanced**: it does everything the Standard notebook does. The Batch notebook has its own [guide](batch/README.md).
Feature comparison | Feature | Advanced | Standard | Batch | |:--|:--:|:--:|:--:| | Proteins and multi-chain complexes | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | Small-molecule ligands (SMILES or CCD code) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | Binding affinity | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | DNA and RNA | ✅ | – | ✅ | | Uploaded MSA (`.a3m`) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | Structural templates | ✅ | – | ✅ | | Covalent bonds, pocket and contact constraints | ✅ | – | – | | Modified residues, cyclic peptides | ✅ | – | – | | Import chains and ligands from a PDB or mmCIF file | ✅ | ✅ | – | | Many jobs from a CSV or FASTA file, with ranking | – | – | ✅ | | 3-D viewer and HTML report per job | ✅ | ✅ | summary table |
## What you get | Input builder | Live run panel | |:--|:--| | ![Input builder with a protein, a ligand with its 2-D drawing, and the live summary](assets/ui/input-builder.png) | ![Run panel with phase tracker, timer and log, while running and after a failure](assets/ui/run-panel.png) | | **Result card** | **Run settings** | | ![Result card with confidence scores and the binding-affinity summary](assets/ui/result-card.png) | ![Quality presets and run settings](assets/ui/run-settings.png) | - **A guided form** that checks your input as you type: sequences, chain IDs, SMILES (with a 2-D drawing) and CCD codes, with a live summary and YAML preview. - **Confidence scores** that are easy to read: per-residue pLDDT, the predicted aligned error (PAE) with chain-to-chain blocks, ipTM and interface summaries. - **Binding affinity** for small-molecule ligands: the probability that the ligand binds, and the predicted IC50 in µM and nM, with pIC50 and an approximate ΔG. - **Several samples per job** if you want them, with the spread across samples reported. - **A self-contained HTML report** for each job: figures, the 3-D structure, tables and everything needed to reproduce the run. - **Clear failures:** when a run fails, the notebook names the likely cause and how to fix it. - **Light and dark themes**, and a layout that works on screens from 360 px wide. ## Reading the results | Quantity | What it means | |:--|:--| | **pLDDT** (0 to 100) | Confidence per residue: above 90 very high, 70 to 90 high, 50 to 70 low, below 50 very low. Ligands and modified residues get one value per heavy atom. | | **PAE** (Å) | Expected position error between two residues. It is asymmetric (row: aligned residue, column: scored residue); blocks between two chains show how confident the interface is. | | **Confidence score, pTM, ipTM** | Boltz's ranking metrics. Sample 0 is the best-ranked sample. | | **Binding probability** | How likely the ligand is a binder. Use it to separate binders from decoys. | | **Predicted affinity** | log10 of the IC50 in µM: −2 is about 10 nM, 0 is 1 µM, 1 is 10 µM. Use it to rank close analogues, not to compare unrelated compounds. Meaningful for small molecules only. | ## Requirements - A Google account and a **GPU runtime** in Colab (T4 or better; use an L4 or A100 for large complexes). - About **6 GB** of model files are downloaded once per session. - The notebook installs the engine for you: `boltz 2.2.1` on Python 3.10 to 3.12, and the `boltz-community 2.10.12` fork on Python 3.13 runtimes, where the official package is not available yet. - Protein sequences are sent to the ColabFold MSA server to build alignments, unless you upload your own MSA or choose single-sequence mode. ## Troubleshooting | Problem | What to do | |:--|:--| | **CUDA out of memory** | Lower *Max MSA sequences* (for example 256), use 1 sample, or switch to an L4 or A100 runtime. | | **MSA server failed or timed out** | Try again later, upload an `.a3m` file, or choose single-sequence mode. | | **Invalid SMILES or unknown CCD code** | The form checks both while you type; fix the entry it marks. | | **A template cannot be read** | Use the template's `.cif` file, or a `.pdb` file with SEQRES records (files written by Boltz itself have none). The form warns about this when you upload. | | **Low pLDDT everywhere** | Often a disordered region or single-sequence mode: provide an MSA or a template. | Every failed run shows a likely cause and a fix. For an analysis that does not line up with the predicted files, run `python -m boltz2nb.doctor /content/boltz_data/` and include its output in an [issue](https://github.com/AtharvaTilewale/boltz2-notebook/issues). ## Privacy Your inputs stay in your Colab runtime, except for the MSA request (your protein sequences go to the ColabFold server), the check of CCD codes with the PDB, and usage reports, which help improve the tool and contain no personal data. Usage reports are on by default: untick `SEND_USAGE_STATS` in the first cell to turn them off. See [PRIVACY.md](docs/PRIVACY.md) for details. ## Run it on your own machine
Install and run without Colab ```bash git clone https://github.com/AtharvaTilewale/boltz2-notebook && cd boltz2-notebook pip install -e ".[ligand,viewer]" "boltz[cuda]==2.2.1" export BOLTZ2NB_BASE_DIR=$PWD/boltz_data # where params.yaml, run_params.txt and the results live python - <<'PY' from boltz2nb.yaml_builder import build_yaml, write_yaml, simple_spec from boltz2nb.run_params import serialize_run_params, DEFAULTS write_yaml(build_yaml(simple_spec("MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQLEERLGL", ligand_smiles="CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O", affinity=True)), "boltz_data/params.yaml") open("boltz_data/run_params.txt", "w").write(serialize_run_params(dict(DEFAULTS, job_name="demo"))) PY python scripts/common/Boltz_Run.py && python scripts/common/analysis.py # the report is written to boltz_data/demo/analysis/ ```
Run settings and their defaults | Setting | Default | Range | Meaning | |:--|:--|:--|:--| | Recycling steps | 3 | 1 to 20 | Refinement passes of the trunk | | Sampling steps | 200 | 10 to 1000 | Diffusion steps per sample | | Diffusion samples | 1 | 1 to 25 | Structures per job; 3 or more give a spread estimate | | Step scale | 1.638 | 0.5 to 5 | Lower values give more diverse samples | | Max MSA sequences | 8192 | 1 to 16384 | Depth cap of the alignment | | Subsample MSA | on, 1024 | | Faster and lighter on memory | | MSA pairing | greedy | greedy, complete | How chains of a complex are paired | | Steering potentials | off | | Physics-based potentials during sampling | The **Fast** preset uses 2 recycling steps, 50 sampling steps and an MSA depth of 256; **Scientific** uses 5 recycling steps, 5 samples and the steering potentials.
How it works The notebooks are thin shells. Cell 1 clones a pinned release tag of this repository and installs the `boltz2nb` package and the Boltz engine; the other cells run three scripts that call into the package: | Cell | Script | What it does | |:--|:--|:--| | Generate Parameters | `scripts/v1` or `scripts/v2/param_gen.py` | The input builder; writes `params.yaml` and `run_params.txt` | | Run Boltz2 Engine | `scripts/common/Boltz_Run.py` | Builds the `boltz predict` command, shows live progress and the result card; never overwrites an existing job folder | | Analyse Results | `scripts/common/analysis.py` | Maps confidence values to residues, computes interface and ensemble statistics, writes `analysis/_report.html` and `summary.json` | Each job folder also keeps `boltz.log`, `status.json` and `run_context.json` (engine, PyTorch and CUDA versions, GPU, the exact command and the input). The package, its tests and the release process are described in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).
## Documentation - [Use cases](https://atharvatilewale.github.io/boltz2-notebook/docs/use-cases.html) and [FAQ](https://atharvatilewale.github.io/boltz2-notebook/docs/faq.html) on the website - [Batch guide](batch/README.md): high-throughput screens from CSV or FASTA - [Changelog](releases/CHANGELOG.md) and [version table](releases/version_table.md) - [Privacy](docs/PRIVACY.md) and, for maintainers, [receiving usage reports](docs/TELEMETRY.md) - [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) and the [verification log](docs/VERIFICATION.md) ## Citation If Boltz2-Notebook helps your work, please cite the preprint, and Boltz-2 for the model: ```bibtex @article{Tilewale2026.09.18.752645, author = {Tilewale, Atharva and Patel, Dhaval}, title = {Boltz2-Notebook: An Interactive Google Colab Platform for Diffusion-Based Biomolecular Structure and Binding Affinity Prediction using the Boltz2 model}, journal = {bioRxiv}, year = {2026}, doi = {10.64898/2026.09.18.752645}, url = {https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2026/09/24/2026.09.18.752645}, publisher = {Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory} } @article{Passaro2025, author = {Passaro, Saro and Corso, Gabriele and Wohlwend, Jeremy and others}, title = {Boltz-2: Towards Accurate and Efficient Binding Affinity Prediction}, journal = {bioRxiv}, year = {2025}, doi = {10.1101/2025.06.14.659707} } @article{Wohlwend2024, author = {Wohlwend, Jeremy and Corso, Gabriele and Passaro, Saro and others}, title = {Boltz-1: Democratizing Biomolecular Interaction Modeling}, journal = {bioRxiv}, year = {2024}, doi = {10.1101/2024.11.19.624167} } ``` ## Authors and acknowledgements Developed by [Atharva Tilewale](https://github.com/AtharvaTilewale) and Dr. Dhaval Patel at Gujarat Biotechnology University. # MUC2 Glycosylation Analysis
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) [![Python 3.10+](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.10+-3776AB?logo=python&logoColor=white)](https://www.python.org/) [![Jupyter](https://img.shields.io/badge/Jupyter-Notebooks-F37626?logo=jupyter&logoColor=white)](https://jupyter.org/) [![Open Source](https://img.shields.io/badge/Open%20Source-%E2%9D%A4-red.svg)](https://github.com/jkamantey/muc2-glycosylation-analysis) [![AMBER](https://img.shields.io/badge/Force%20Field-AMBER-green.svg)]() **Open-source MD analysis pipeline for the MUC2 mucin long PTS domain** *How O-glycosylation reshapes backbone mechanics, polymer properties, and ligand interaction capacity*
--- ## Table of Contents - [Overview](#overview) - [Systems](#systems) - [Analysis Pipeline](#analysis-pipeline) - [Notebooks](#notebooks) - [Key Findings](#key-findings) - [Installation](#installation) - [Data](#data) - [Citation](#citation) - [License](#license) - [Author](#author) --- ## Overview **MUC2** is the dominant gel-forming glycoprotein of the intestinal mucus layer. Its **long PTS (Pro-Thr-Ser) domain** — a tandem-repeat intrinsically disordered region carrying up to 30 O-linked glycan chains — is responsible for the mucus gel's unique mechanical properties: rigidity, hydration, and selective permeability. This repository provides a complete, reproducible computational pipeline that answers two connected questions: > **1.** What are the intrinsic biophysical and polymer properties of the MUC2 PTS backbone? > > **2.** How do O-glycosylation and ligand interactions progressively reshape those properties? The pipeline moves from local backbone geometry (per-residue bending, dihedral angles) through global chain mechanics (persistence length, radius of gyration) to correlated dynamics and free energy landscapes — building a full structural picture of how glycosylation transforms a flexible disordered peptide into a stiff, rod-like mucin fibre. --- ## Systems Three glycosylation states are compared across **~10,800 ns** of all-atom MD simulation: | System | Description | Colour | Simulation | |--------|-------------|--------|------------| | **Non-glycosylated** | Naked PTS backbone, no O-glycans | ![#A23B72](https://placehold.co/12x12/A23B72/A23B72.png) `#A23B72` | 3 × 1200 ns | | **Mid-level Glycosylated** | Partial O-glycosylation | ![#2E86AB](https://placehold.co/12x12/2E86AB/2E86AB.png) `#2E86AB` | 3 × 1200 ns | | **Ext. Glycosylated** | Full / dense O-glycosylation | ![#F18F01](https://placehold.co/12x12/F18F01/F18F01.png) `#F18F01` | 3 × 1200 ns | > 2381 frames per system · 1.2 ns/frame · AMBER force field · explicit solvent (TIP3P) --- ## Analysis Pipeline ``` ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ STAGE 1 — Biophysical │ │ Characterise the MUC2 backbone │ ├──────────────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────────────┤ │ Local geometry │ Global polymer │ Conformational sampling │ │ │ mechanics │ │ │ · Cα curvature │ · Rg, ETE │ · PCA (PC1, PC2) │ │ · Pre-glycan │ · Persistence │ · Free energy surface │ │ bending │ length │ · Dihedral distributions │ │ · φ/ψ angles │ · RMSF │ · Secondary structure │ │ · Twist profile │ │ │ └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘ ↓ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ STAGE 2 — Dynamics & Interactions │ │ How glycosylation reshapes properties & binding │ ├──────────────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────────────┤ │ Correlated │ Interaction │ Thermodynamics │ │ motions │ network │ │ │ │ │ │ │ · DCCM │ · H-bond │ · PMF / FES │ │ · Cross-norm │ occupancy │ · Conformational │ │ DCCM │ · Ligand │ barriers │ │ │ accessibility │ │ └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘ ``` --- ## Notebooks ### Stage 1 — Biophysical Properties | Notebook | Description | |----------|-------------| | [`radius_of_curvature.ipynb`](radius_of_curvature.ipynb) | Cα interior virtual bond-angle curvature · per-residue bending profiles · pre-glycan structural hotspot analysis · bimodal distribution characterisation | | [`rmsf_comparison.ipynb`](rmsf_comparison.ipynb) | Per-residue RMSF across all three systems · identifies stiffened and mobilised regions | | [`plot_physical_vars.ipynb`](plot_physical_vars.ipynb) | PCA coloured by Rg · ETE · curvature · persistence length · free energy surface · Pearson correlations with PC axes | | [`persistence_length.ipynb`](persistence_length.ipynb) | Worm-like chain (WLC) fit · sliding-window Lp · stiffness comparison across glycosylation states | | [`phi_psi_bend_analysis.ipynb`](phi_psi_bend_analysis.ipynb) | Ramachandran scatter from mean structures · bend redistribution profiles · Cα dihedral twist analysis | | [`dihedral_distribution.ipynb`](dihedral_distribution.ipynb) | Backbone φ/ψ dihedral distributions · conformational basin populations | | [`secondary_structure.ipynb`](secondary_structure.ipynb) | DSSP secondary structure per residue per frame · PPII / coil content vs glycosylation | ### Stage 2 — Dynamics, Correlations & Interactions | Notebook | Description | |----------|-------------| | [`dccm_glyc_noglyc.ipynb`](dccm_glyc_noglyc.ipynb) | Dynamic cross-correlation matrix (DCCM) · glyc vs non-glyc | | [`dccm_comparison.ipynb`](dccm_comparison.ipynb) | DCCM comparison across all three glycosylation states | | [`dccm_crossnorm.ipynb`](dccm_crossnorm.ipynb) | Cross-normalised DCCM · isolates changes in correlation pattern independent of fluctuation magnitude | | [`hbond_analysis.ipynb`](hbond_analysis.ipynb) | Intra-chain and chain–solvent H-bond occupancy · backbone donor/acceptor accessibility for ligand binding | | [`pmf_ref_formula.ipynb`](pmf_ref_formula.ipynb) | Potential of mean force (PMF) along PC1/PC2 · reference formula | | [`pmf_corrected_formula.ipynb`](pmf_corrected_formula.ipynb) | PMF · corrected formula · conformational stability comparison | ### PCA & Conformational Sampling | Notebook | Description | |----------|-------------| | [`muc2_newsystem.ipynb`](muc2_newsystem.ipynb) | Combined PCA · glycosylated + non-glycosylated · shared conformational space | | [`muc2_noglycans.ipynb`](muc2_noglycans.ipynb) | PCA · non-glycosylated system only | | [`pca_dccm_noglyc_domains.ipynb`](pca_dccm_noglyc_domains.ipynb) | PCA + DCCM by domain · non-glycosylated | | [`pca_dccm_normal_domains.ipynb`](pca_dccm_normal_domains.ipynb) | PCA + DCCM by domain · glycosylated | | [`pca_last400_comparison.ipynb`](pca_last400_comparison.ipynb) | PCA of last 400 ns per run · convergence check | --- ## Key Findings
1. The sequence pre-encodes structural hotspots at glycan sites 25 out of 30 pre-glycan positions already form a local bending peak in the **non-glycosylated** chain — before any glycan is attached. The backbone geometry is shaped by the amino acid sequence to anticipate glycosylation. The 5 non-rising sites are all **Glycine**, falling at exactly position 6 of every 6-residue tandem repeat unit.
2. Glycine acts as the periodic conformational hinge Glycine is the only amino acid with no side chain, giving it exceptional conformational freedom. It cannot hold the backbone in the extended geometry that Thr, Ile, Val, and Pro enforce — instead it dips into a more kinked state. This makes it the structurally weakest point in each repeat unit, and the site of the **largest glycan-driven conformational rescue** (up to +15.6° at a single Gly site under full glycosylation).
3. Glycosylation redistributes bending rather than uniformly stiffening The total summed bending across the chain is similar between systems, but its spatial distribution changes: some residues become more extended while others become more kinked. This redistribution — not simple global stiffening — is the dominant mechanical effect of glycosylation.
4. Bimodal angle distributions signal conformational switching Rather than shifting all pre-glycan residues to a new single preferred angle, glycosylation splits the population into two distinct peaks. The backbone switches between two energy minima — a behaviour that at the macroscopic scale underpins the viscoelastic (simultaneously solid-like and liquid-like) mechanics of mucus gels.
5. Long-range correlated motions increase with glycosylation DCCM analysis shows that glycosylation introduces longer-range dynamic correlations along the chain. This has direct consequences for ligand interactions: a ligand binding at one region can propagate its structural effect further along the chain in the glycosylated system than in the naked backbone.
--- ## Key Results Table | Property | Non-glycosylated | Mid-glycosylated | Ext. glycosylated | |----------|:---:|:---:|:---:| | Mean Cα bend angle (°) | ~116–120 | ~119–124 | ~122–128 | | Gly-site Δ angle from non-glyc (°) | — | up to +10 | up to **+16** | | Pre-glycan angle distribution | unimodal · narrow | bimodal · broader | bimodal · broad | | Bend redistribution | baseline | partial | strong | | Chain stiffness (Lp) | lowest | intermediate | highest | | Long-range DCCM correlations | weakest | intermediate | strongest | --- ## Installation ```bash # Clone the repository git clone https://github.com/jkamantey/muc2-glycosylation-analysis.git cd muc2-glycosylation-analysis # Create a conda environment conda create -n muc2_analysis python=3.10 conda activate muc2_analysis # Install dependencies pip install numpy scipy matplotlib pandas jupyter mdanalysis ``` ### Running a notebook interactively ```bash jupyter notebook ``` ### Running a notebook non-interactively ```bash jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute \ --ExecutePreprocessor.kernel_name=anaconda-base \ --ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=600 \ --inplace .ipynb ``` ### Setting your data path Each notebook has a `BASE` variable near the top pointing to the local data directory. Update it to match your system before running: ```python BASE = '/path/to/your/data/' ``` --- ## Data Trajectory files (`.xtc`), topology files (`.prmtop`), and raw data arrays (`.dat`, `.csv`) are **not included** in this repository due to file size. The notebooks load data via relative paths from the `BASE` variable. To reproduce the analysis, you will need: - AMBER topology (`.prmtop`) for each system - Aligned trajectory files (`.xtc`) for each of the three independent runs - Pre-computed curvature, PCA, and physical variable data files Contact the author if you are interested in accessing the simulation data. --- ## Citation If you use this code or analysis pipeline in your work, please cite: ```bibtex @software{mantey2026muc2, author = {Mantey, Joshua}, title = {MUC2 Glycosylation Analysis: MD Simulation Pipeline}, year = {2026}, publisher = {GitHub}, url = {https://github.com/jkamantey/muc2-glycosylation-analysis}, institution = {Northeastern University} } ``` --- ## License This project is licensed under the **MIT License** — free to use, modify, and distribute with attribution. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) for full details. --- ## Author **Joshua Mantey** Northeastern University [mantey.j@northeastern.edu](mailto:mantey.j@northeastern.edu) *Computational biophysics · MUC2 mucin glycobiology · Intrinsically disordered proteins · Molecular dynamics*
