## 是什么

GAQA 是一个基于 Nextflow DSL2 的流水线，用于大规模蛋白质结构预测、固有无序分析以及基因组注释质量评估。它整合了 Protenix（结构预测）、Metapredict（无序预测）、PSAURON（编码序列质量评估）和 InterProScan（功能结构域注释），并针对 HPC 环境（支持 SLURM）和 GPU 加速进行了优化。

## 亮点

- **模块化与可扩展性**：四个分析分支（Protenix、Metapredict、PSAURON、InterProScan）可独立开关，支持按需组合，便于在资源受限或特定分析场景下灵活配置。
- **HPC 并行化**：通过 Nextflow 的 chunking 机制（基于贪心 LPT 装箱算法）实现序列级并行，平衡计算负载，尤其适合大规模蛋白质组。
- **多输入支持**：支持多个 FASTA 文件输入，可生成独立 PDF 报告或合并报告，便于跨物种比较。
- **稳定的输出格式**：统一的单行 TSV 摘要，列结构固定（未运行的分支留空），便于下游批量聚合分析。
- **容器化部署**：提供预构建的 Singularity/Apptainer 镜像，简化依赖管理，支持本地和集群环境。

## 为何对本课题有用

GAQA 直接针对 IDR/IDP 研究中的关键计算需求：

- **无序预测集成**：通过 Metapredict 提供 GPU 加速的固有无序预测，可直接用于大规模蛋白质组的 IDR 注释，为 IDP 功能研究提供基础数据。
- **结构-无序关联分析**：将 Protenix 的 pLDDT 分数与 Metapredict 的无序分数结合，生成无序着色的 GMM 散点图，可揭示结构域与无序区域的分布模式，对理解 IDP 的构象系综和相分离倾向有参考价值。
- **注释质量评估**：PSAURON 和 InterProScan 的集成有助于识别假基因或错误注释，确保下游 IDP 分析的输入数据质量。
- **可迁移的流水线架构**：其模块化设计可作为构建 IDP 特定分析流水线的模板，例如将 Metapredict 替换为其他无序预测器，或添加 IDP 构象采样步骤。

## 怎么用

- **安装**：需要 Nextflow ≥ 23、Java 8+、Singularity/Apptainer。克隆仓库后，运行 `bin/download_containers.sh` 下载预构建镜像，或使用 `nox -s build_apptainer` 本地构建。
- **运行**：
  ```bash
  nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm --fasta example.fasta --chunk_size 100 --singularity_image_dir /path/to/images
  ```
  可通过 `--run_protenix`、`--run_metapredict`、`--run_psauron`、`--run_interpro` 控制分支。
- **输入**：FASTA 文件（蛋白质序列），支持多个文件或 glob。
- **输出**：`results/` 目录下包含 PDF 报告、PNG 图、pLDDT PKL 文件、CSV 文件及 TSV 摘要。
- **调试**：测试文件 `tests/test_balance_chunks.py` 可用于验证 chunking 逻辑；可单独运行 `bin/plot_*.py` 脚本进行断点调试。
- **GPU 需求**：Protenix、Metapredict、PSAURON 推荐 GPU 加速，InterProScan 可 CPU 运行。

## 核心 idea

GAQA 的核心方法学在于**通过模块化流水线整合多种互补的蛋白质特征（结构、无序、功能注释），并利用贪心装箱算法实现负载均衡的并行计算**，从而在保持高精度的同时实现大规模蛋白质组的高通量分析。其创新点不在于单一算法，而在于将不同工具无缝集成，并提供统一的比较框架（如参考物种叠加），使注释质量评估变得直观且可扩展。

## 可搬移点

- **LPT 装箱算法**（`bin/balance_chunks.sh`）：可独立提取，用于任何需要负载均衡的序列分块任务，例如 IDP 构象系综的并行采样。
- **pLDDT 提取与 GMM 拟合逻辑**（`bin/process_models.py`、`bin/plot_plddt.py`）：可复用其 pLDDT 分布建模方法，用于分析 IDP 的结构倾向性。
- **Metapredict 集成方式**：可参考其如何调用 Metapredict 并处理输出，用于构建自定义无序预测流水线。
- **参考数据集格式**：`reference/` 下的 CSV/PKL 文件格式可作为 IDP 参考数据集的模板。
- **License**：仓库未明确说明 License，需确认。

**注意**：以上可搬移点基于 README 描述，具体实现细节需查看源码。
readme:
# GAQA — Genome Annotation Quality Assessment

**GAQA**  is a Nextflow pipeline for large-scale
protein structure prediction, intrinsic disorder analysis, and genome
annotation quality assessment using **Protenix**, **Metapredict**,
**PSAURON**, and **InterProScan**.

The code lives in the `genome_annotation_quality_nextflow_pipeline`
repository, and its container images are named `GAQA_*.sif`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Overview

This repository contains a **Nextflow DSL2 pipeline** for:

- Large-scale protein structure prediction using Protenix
- Intrinsic disorder prediction using Metapredict
- Protein-coding sequence quality assessment using PSAURON
- Functional domain annotation and coverage profiling using InterProScan
- Automated chunking and HPC parallelisation
- Model processing and metric extraction
- Comparative plotting against reference proteome datasets
- One-row summary TSV per run, aggregating the headline plot metrics
  across all branches
- Every analysis branch can be switched on or off independently
  (see [Choosing which branches run](#choosing-which-branches-run))
- Several FASTA files in one run, with a PDF report per input and,
  optionally, a combined report that puts every input on the same plots
  (see [Running several FASTA files](#running-several-fasta-files))

The pipeline is designed for HPC environments (SLURM supported)
and supports GPU acceleration where appropriate.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Protenix-Mini Overview

Accurate protein structure prediction is often computationally intensive, limiting scalability for large-scale or real-world applications. Protenix-Mini is a lightweight, optimized variant of the Protenix framework designed to balance computational efficiency with high predictive accuracy. It achieves this through several key architectural refinements: replacing the multi-step AF3 diffusion sampler with a reduced-step Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) sampler to lower inference overhead, pruning non-contributory Transformer components within the pairformer and diffusion modules, and incorporating an ESM-based protein language model to substitute the traditional MSA module—thereby eliminating costly MSA preprocessing. These modifications substantially reduce model complexity and runtime while maintaining high structural fidelity. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate only a minimal 1–5% decrease in performance relative to the full-scale model. Protenix-Mini therefore enables efficient, GPU-accelerated structure prediction suitable for large proteomes and resource-constrained environments, making it well suited for high-throughput genome annotation quality assessment workflows.
## Metapredict Overview

Intrinsically disordered proteins and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) play essential roles in cellular regulation, signaling, phase separation, and molecular recognition. Accurate identification of IDRs directly from sequence is therefore critical for understanding protein function at scale. Metapredict is a state-of-the-art disorder prediction tool designed for both high accuracy and extremely high throughput, enabling proteome-scale analyses in seconds. Developed with usability in mind, Metapredict is distributed as a web server, Python package, command-line interface, and Google Colab notebook. Leveraging deep learning–based predictions trained across diverse datasets, Metapredict V3 enables evolutionary-scale disorder analysis across thousands of proteomes. In this pipeline, Metapredict is integrated as a GPU-accelerated step to generate per-protein disorder metrics and comparative distributions against large multi-species reference datasets, facilitating genome-wide disorder profiling and annotation quality assessment.
## PSAURON Overview

Evaluating the accuracy of protein-coding sequences in genome annotations
is a challenging problem with no broadly applicable universal solution.

PSAURON (Protein Sequence Assessment Using a Reference ORF Network)
is a machine learning–based tool trained on a diverse dataset of over
1000 plant and animal genomes. It assigns a score to coding DNA or protein
sequences reflecting the likelihood that the sequence represents a genuine
protein-coding region.

PSAURON scores enable:

- Genome-wide protein annotation quality assessment
- Rapid identification of potentially spurious protein annotations
- Comparative overlay against large multi-species reference datasets

This pipeline integrates PSAURON scoring directly into structure and
disorder prediction workflows for multi-metric genome annotation QC.

## InterProScan Overview

Functional annotation of protein sequences is a cornerstone of genome
quality assessment. InterProScan integrates fifteen member databases —
including PFAM, PANTHER, GENE3D, SUPERFAMILY, FUNFAM, CDD, SMART, PRINTS,
HAMAP, PIRSF, PIRSR, SFLD, NCBIFAM, PROSITE_PROFILES and PROSITE_PATTERNS —
to assign protein family, domain, and functional site signatures, mapping
them where possible to the unified InterPro classification.

In this pipeline, InterProScan is used to compute two complementary
genome-quality metrics:

- **Per-library coverage**: the percentage of input proteins matched by
  each signature library, plus an overall "any IPR hit" total. This
  reveals which evidence sources are dominant for a given proteome and
  flags annotation gaps relative to reference organisms.
- **Per-protein domain coverage**: for every protein, the fraction of
  residues covered by the union of its IPR-bearing matches (overlapping
  hits merged so residues are not double-counted), giving a length-
  normalised score between 0 and 1. The distribution of this score
  across the proteome is a sensitive indicator of annotation quality —
  proteomes with many short, fragmented, or spurious annotations
  typically show a heavy excess of low-coverage proteins relative to
  well-annotated reference organisms.

The InterProScan branch is **off by default** and is enabled with
`--run_interpro true` (see [Choosing which branches run](#choosing-which-branches-run)).
Because InterProScan is computationally expensive, the pipeline
parallelises it by chunking the input FASTA, running each chunk
independently, and concatenating the per-chunk XML/TSV outputs before
plotting. The number of chunks matches however many chunks the Protenix
branch produced (set by `--chunk_size`); if Protenix is switched off,
it is the FASTA's sequence count divided by `--chunk_size`, rounded up.

Chunking uses greedy longest-processing-time-first (LPT) bin-packing
(`bin/balance_chunks.sh`): sequences are sorted by length descending and
each is assigned to whichever chunk currently has the smallest total
residue count. This keeps per-chunk runtime balanced even when large
multi-domain genes are clustered together in the input FASTA (naive
sequential N-sequences-per-chunk splitting can leave one chunk with
several giant outliers while others sit mostly idle). The assignment is
deterministic — the same input and chunk count always produce the same
chunks.



## Summary Metrics TSV

In addition to the per-branch plots and the PDF report, the pipeline
emits a single-row TSV file for each input
(`results/<dataset>_summary.tsv`) containing the headline numbers used
to construct the plots. This is intended for downstream tabular
aggregation — concatenating the summary TSVs across many runs gives a
single table comparing all queries on the same metrics. With
`--report combined`, the pipeline does this for you:
`results/<combined_name>_summary.tsv` has one row per input.

The TSV always carries the same column schema. Columns for any branch
that was switched off are left blank rather than removed, so the layout
is stable across runs.

| Column                 | Source         | Description                                                                                       |
|------------------------|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `dataset`              | run parameter  | Dataset identifier (the FASTA basename)                                                           |
| `total_proteins`       | pLDDT PKL / FASTA | Number of proteins for which a mean pLDDT was computed; if Protenix is off, the number of sequences in the input FASTA |
| `prop_ge_70`           | Protenix       | Fraction of proteins with mean pLDDT ≥ 70 (y-axis of the GMM scatter plot)                        |
| `gmm_upper_prop`       | Protenix       | Weight of the upper component of a 2-component GMM fitted to the pLDDT distribution, with guided initialisation from the reference species (x-axis of the GMM scatter plot) |
| `disorder_prop_gt_0p5` | Metapredict    | Proportion of proteins with mean disorder score > 0.5                                             |
| `psauron_high_pct`     | PSAURON        | Percentage of proteins with `in-frame_score` ≥ 0.9 (the "High" bar of the PSAURON plot)           |
| `ipr_hit_pct`          | InterProScan   | Percentage of proteins with at least one IPR-bearing hit (the "any IPR hit" total from the InterPro coverage plot). Blank if `--run_interpro` is `false`. |

A single `BUILD_SUMMARY_TSV` process implements this stage. Because DSL2
does not cleanly support optional `path` inputs, `main.nf` passes a
placeholder file from `assets/` (`NO_FILE_PLDDT`, `NO_FILE_METAPREDICT`,
`NO_FILE_PSAURON`, `NO_FILE_IPR_XML`) for each branch that did not run,
and the process leaves the matching flag off the
`bin/build_summary_tsv.py` command line. The same mechanism lets
`PLOT_PLDDT` run without Metapredict; in that case it skips only the
disorder-coloured GMM scatter plot.


## Choosing which branches run

Each of the four analysis branches can be switched on or off
independently. At least one must be on; the pipeline stops with an error
if all four are off. The PDF report and summary TSV only include the
branches that ran.

| Parameter           | Default | Branch                                              |
|---------------------|---------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| `--run_protenix`    | `true`  | Protenix structure prediction and pLDDT plots       |
| `--run_metapredict` | `true`  | Metapredict disorder prediction and plots           |
| `--run_psauron`     | `true`  | PSAURON scoring and plots                           |
| `--run_interpro`    | `false` | InterProScan. `true` runs it; a path to an InterProScan XML file plots that XML instead |

Values are case-insensitive (`true`/`false`, `yes`/`no`, `1`/`0`).
For example, to skip the GPU-heavy Protenix step and run only the
sequence-based branches plus InterProScan:

```bash
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm --fasta example.fasta --run_protenix false --run_interpro true --interpro_data /path/to/interpro_data
```



## Installation Instructions

Follow these steps to install and set up **GAQA**:

### 1. Install Nextflow

Nextflow is required to run the pipeline.

```bash

curl -s https://get.nextflow.io | bash

mv nextflow ~/bin/

nextflow -version
```

> Ensure `~/bin` is in your `PATH` or adjust the path accordingly.

---

### 2. Install Java (if needed)

Nextflow requires Java 8+:

```bash

sudo apt-get install openjdk-11-jdk


java -version
```

---

### 3. Download the Pipeline Repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/mesdaghi/genome_annotation_quality_nextflow_pipeline
cd genome_annotation_quality_nextflow_pipeline
```

---

### 4. Setup Singularity/ Apptainer Images

There are two options for setting up the Singularity/Apptainer images required for the pipeline:

#### 4.1 Use Pre-Built Images

The pre-built images are hosted on GitHub Container Registry and can be pulled directly using the download_containers.sh script:

First, make the script executable:
```bash
chmod +x bin/download_containers.sh
```

Make sure APPTAINER_TMP is set to a directory with sufficient space for the images, then run the script to download the images:
```bash
export APPTAINER_TMP=/path/to/temp_directory
mkdir -p APPTAINER_TMP
```

Then run the script to download the images:
```bash
bin/download_containers.sh /path/to/singularity_image_directory
```

#### 4.2 Build Images Locally

If you prefer to build the images locally or are a developer making modifications, you can build the images using a nox session. First, install pipx if you don't have it already:

```bash
python3 -m pip install --user pipx
python3 -m pipx ensurepath
```

Then install nox:

```bash
pipx install nox
```


Finally, build the singularity/apptainer images:

```bash
nox -s build_apptainer -- --output /path/to/singularity_images
```
### 5. Download InterProScan Data

The exact steps for downloading InterProScan data can be found here [InterProScan Data Download](https://interproscan-docs.readthedocs.io/en/v5/HowToUseViaContainer.html). But, in short, you can download the data using the following commands


```bash
curl -O http://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/software/unix/iprscan/5/5.78-109.0/alt/interproscan-data-5.78-109.0.tar.gz

tar -pxzf interproscan-data-5.78-109.0.tar.gz
```

### 6. Run a Test Pipeline

Please specifiy the path to your singularity images directory in the singularity.config file before running the pipeline. (or as a parameter `--singularity_image_dir /path/to/singularity_images`)

There are two profiles available for testing:
1. 'singularity_local' — runs the pipeline locally using Singularity containers
2. 'singularity_slurm' — runs the pipeline on an HPC cluster with SLURM, using Singularity containers

```bash
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm --fasta example.fasta --chunk_size 100 --singularity_image_dir /path/to/singularity_images

```
If using InterProScan, please specify the path to your InterProScan data directory in the singularity.config file before running the pipeline. (or as a parameter `--interpro_data /path/to/interpro_data`) For example:

```bash
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm --fasta example.fasta --chunk_size 100 --singularity_image_dir /path/to/singularity_images --run_interpro true --interpro_data /path/to/interpro_data/interproscan-5.77-108.0/data/
```

- `--fasta` : Input FASTA file(s): a path, a glob (quote it), or a comma-separated list  
- `--fasta_list` : Text file listing input FASTA files, one per line (optional, instead of or as well as `--fasta`)  
- `--report` : `separate` (default) = one PDF per input; `combined` = also a combined PDF comparing all inputs  
- `--chunk_size` : Number of sequences per Protenix chunk  
- `--singularity_image_dir` : Path to directory containing  
Singularity images (optional if set in config)
`--protenix_cache` : Path to Protenix cache directory (optional, can also be set via nextflow.config)
`--run_protenix` : Run the Protenix branch (optional, default: true)
`--run_metapredict` : Run the Metapredict branch (optional, default: true)
`--run_psauron` : Run the PSAURON branch (optional, default: true)
`--run_interpro` : Enable InterPro branch. `true` = run InterProScan; `/path/to/x.xml` = plot only (optional, default: false)
`--interpro_data` : Path to InterProScan data directory (optional, can also be set via nextflow.config)

All output (plots, PKL files, CSVs) will be stored under `results/`.


---

### Notes

- Make sure your environments are accessible on the compute nodes.  
- Set `--protenix_cache` (or `PROTENIX_CACHE`) before running Protenix predictions; not needed with `--run_protenix false`.  


## Features

### Structure Prediction (Protenix)

- On by default; skip with `--run_protenix false`

- FASTA → Protenix JSON conversion
- JSON chunk splitting for parallel inference
- GPU-accelerated Protenix prediction
- Automatic model collection and aggregation
- pLDDT extraction into PKL datasets
- Distribution plotting vs reference organisms
- Disorder-coloured GMM scatter when Metapredict also runs (skipped
  otherwise)

### Disorder Prediction (Metapredict)

- On by default; skip with `--run_metapredict false`

- GPU-accelerated disorder prediction
- Automatic overlay vs reference proteome disorder database
- Histogram and KDE density plots

### Protein-Coding Quality Assessment (PSAURON)

- On by default; skip with `--run_psauron false`

- GPU-accelerated PSAURON scoring
- Overlay of new dataset vs precomputed multi-species reference
- Histogram and KDE density plots
- Automated integration into Nextflow workflow

### Functional Domain Annotation (InterProScan)

- Off by default; FASTA-driven InterProScan branch enabled with `--run_interpro true`
- Automatic chunking and parallel execution across HPC compute nodes
- Concatenation of per-chunk XML/TSV outputs into a single result
- Per-library coverage bar chart with the query highlighted alongside
  five reference model organisms
- Per-protein merged-domain coverage violin/box plot showing the
  distribution of residue-level IPR coverage across the proteome
- Tab-separated summary table of per-species coverage metrics
- Acceptance of a precomputed XML via `--run_interpro /path/to/xml`,
  skipping the (expensive) InterProScan step

                              FASTA
                /        |          |          \
               /         |          |           \
          PROTENIX  METAPREDICT  PSAURON  INTERPROSCAN
              |          |          |           |
           pLDDT PKL    CSV        CSV       XML / TSV
              |          |          |           |
          PLOT_PLDDT  PLOT_META  PLOT_PSAURON  PLOT_INTERPRO
              |          |          |           |
             PNG        PNG        PNG     PNG ×2 + TSV
                \        |          |           /
                 \       |          |          /
                            FINAL REPORT (PDF)
                                  +
                       BUILD_SUMMARY_TSV  →  <dataset>_summary.tsv

With several input FASTA files, the steps above run once per input.
With `--report combined`, every input is also drawn on shared plots,
which are gathered into `<combined_name>_report.pdf`, and the per-input
summary rows are joined into `<combined_name>_summary.tsv`.

Every branch is optional. Protenix, Metapredict and PSAURON run by
default; InterProScan is off by default. The report and summary TSV
include only the branches that ran.

## Running the Pipeline

### Basic Run

```bash
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm --fasta after_461.fasta --chunk_size 100
```

`main.nf` is in the `genome_annotation_quality_nextflow_pipeline/`
subfolder, so run from there or give its full path.

### Parameters

| Parameter              | Description                                                                       |
|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| --fasta                | Input FASTA file(s): a path, a glob (in quotes), or a comma-separated list        |
| --fasta_list           | Text file with one FASTA path (or glob) per line; `#` lines and blank lines are ignored |
| --report               | `separate` (default): one PDF per input. `combined`: also one PDF with every input on shared plots |
| --combined_name        | Name used for the combined outputs (default: `combined`)                          |
| --chunk_size           | Sequences per Protenix chunk (default: 100). Also sets the InterProScan chunk count |
| --run_protenix         | Run the Protenix branch (default: `true`)                                         |
| --run_metapredict      | Run the Metapredict branch (default: `true`)                                      |
| --run_psauron          | Run the PSAURON branch (default: `true`)                                          |
| --run_interpro         | InterPro branch. `true` = run InterProScan; `/path/to/x.xml` = plot only (default: `false`) |
| --interpro_data        | Path to InterProScan data directory (needed with `--run_interpro true`)           |
| --protenix_cache       | Path to Protenix cache directory (needed with Protenix)                           |
| --singularity_image_dir| Path to the Singularity/Apptainer images                                          |
| --ipr_reference_json   | Path to reference model-organism JSON (default: `reference/ipr_coverage.json`)    |

### Running several FASTA files

Give several inputs with `--fasta` (comma-separated, or a quoted glob),
with `--fasta_list` (a text file, one path per line), or with both;
a file named twice is only run once.

```bash
# Comma-separated list
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm \
    --fasta /data/strainA.faa,/data/strainB.faa,/data/strainC.faa

# Glob (keep the quotes so the shell doesn't expand it)
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm \
    --fasta "/data/predicted_genes/*.faa"

# List file
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm \
    --fasta_list inputs.txt
```

An example `inputs.txt`:

```text
# one FASTA per line; blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored
/data/predicted_genes/GCA_000599445.1.faa
/data/predicted_genes/GCA_900044135.1.faa
/data/other/strain_x.faa
```

Relative paths in `--fasta` and `--fasta_list` are resolved from the
directory you launch the pipeline in, so absolute paths are safest.

Each input is named after its file name without the extension
(`GCA_000599445.1.faa` → `GCA_000599445.1`), and every output file
carries that name, so the inputs must have different file names. The
pipeline stops with an error listing any clashes.

**Reports**

- `--report separate` (default): one `<dataset>_report.pdf` and one
  `<dataset>_summary.tsv` per input.
- `--report combined`: the per-input files above, plus
  `<combined_name>_report.pdf`, in which each plot shows every input
  together against the reference organisms, and
  `<combined_name>_summary.tsv`, with one row per input. Set the name
  with `--combined_name` (default: `combined`).

```bash
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm \
    --fasta_list inputs.txt \
    --report combined \
    --combined_name fusarium_strains
```

In the combined plots, each input is a coloured line (pLDDT and
Metapredict densities), a red-ringed labelled point (GMM scatter), or
its own bar group or violin after the reference species (PSAURON and
InterPro). Inputs appear in alphabetical order. The pLDDT scatter
coloured by disorder needs Metapredict to have run.

`--run_interpro /path/to/x.xml` (plot a supplied XML) works with a
single input only; use `--run_interpro true` to run InterProScan on
several inputs.

### Running a subset of branches

```bash
# Skip Protenix (the GPU-heavy step); run Metapredict and PSAURON only
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm \
    --fasta after_461.fasta \
    --run_protenix false

# PSAURON only
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm \
    --fasta after_461.fasta \
    --run_protenix false \
    --run_metapredict false

# InterProScan only
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm \
    --fasta after_461.fasta \
    --run_protenix false \
    --run_metapredict false \
    --run_psauron false \
    --run_interpro true \
    --interpro_data /path/to/interpro_data
```

### Running with the InterProScan branch

The InterProScan branch is opt-in. By default it is disabled. It can be
combined with any of the other branches.

```bash
# Full branch — runs InterProScan from scratch on the input FASTA
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm \
    --fasta after_461.fasta \
    --run_interpro true

# Plot-only — skip the (expensive) InterProScan step and reuse a
# previously generated XML, paired with the dataset's FASTA
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm \
    --fasta after_461.fasta \
    --run_interpro /path/to/precomputed_interproscan_output.xml

# Override the reference model-organism dataset
nextflow run main.nf -profile singularity_slurm \
    --fasta after_461.fasta \
    --run_interpro true \
    --ipr_reference_json /path/to/custom_ipr_coverage.json
```

## Example Output Images

### pLDDT Distribution Example


![pLDDT KDE Example](plddt_density_scipy_after_461.png)
## Proteome Structural Confidence Landscape

This plot positions each species according to two complementary measures of proteome structural quality derived from AlphaFold pLDDT scores, allowing the query proteome to be interpreted in the context of well-characterised reference organisms.

![Proteome Structural Confidence Landscape](plddt_gmm_scatter.png)

### Axes

**X-axis — GMM Upper Component Proportion**
Each species' pLDDT distribution is modelled as a two-component Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), capturing the characteristic bimodal shape seen in most proteomes — a lower-confidence disordered peak and a higher-confidence structured peak. The x-axis shows the weight of the upper (higher pLDDT) component, i.e. the proportion of proteins belonging to the high-confidence structured peak. Species further right have a greater fraction of their proteome in the structured, high-confidence GMM component.

**Y-axis — Proportion ≥70 pLDDT**
A simpler, threshold-based measure of the same concept — the fraction of proteins with a mean pLDDT ≥ 70, a commonly used cutoff distinguishing confidently modelled from poorly modelled regions. The two axes are expected to correlate, but divergence between them can indicate unusual distributional shapes.

### Colour — Skew
Points are coloured by the skewness of each species' pLDDT distribution. Negative skew (purple) indicates a distribution pulled toward lower pLDDT values, typical of proteomes with a large disordered or low-complexity fraction. Positive skew (yellow) indicates a tail toward higher confidence values.

### Red circle — Query species
The input dataset is highlighted with a red circle and bold label, allowing its structural quality profile to be interpreted relative to reference proteomes. Its position gives an intuitive indication of whether the proteome resembles organisms with high structural coverage (top right, e.g. vertebrates) or those with more disordered or low-confidence proteomes (bottom left, e.g. parasitic protozoa).

### GMM initialisation
To ensure consistent and comparable fits across species, the GMM for each species is initialised using parameters averaged from six reference species — *Drosophila melanogaster*, *Homo sapiens*, *Rattus norvegicus*, *Mus musculus*, *Pan troglodytes*, and *Arabidopsis thaliana* — rather than random starting points.

### PSAURON Example

![PSAURON Example](psauron_categorical_distribution_new.png)

### InterPro Per-Library Coverage Example

This plot shows the percentage of input proteins matched by each
InterProScan signature library, with the query species highlighted on the
right. The final dark "Total (any IPR hit)" bar gives the headline
overall coverage figure (e.g. 58.4% for *Arabidopsis thaliana*).

![InterPro Per-Library Coverage Example](query_ipr_coverage.png)

#### How to interpret
- **Per-library bars** show what fraction of the proteome is matched by
  each library individually. A protein hit by both PFAM and PANTHER will
  contribute to both bars — these are not stacked, so summing across
  libraries does not give the total.
- **Total bar** shows the percentage of proteins with at least one hit
  from any IPR-bearing library — the canonical "InterPro coverage" figure.
- **Library order** is determined by aggregate hit count across all
  species in the reference set, so the most informative libraries
  appear leftmost.

### InterPro Per-Protein Coverage Distribution Example

This plot shows the distribution of length-normalised IPR coverage
across every protein in each proteome. For each protein, all IPR-bearing
hits are merged (overlapping intervals counted once) and the covered
residues divided by the protein length to give a score between 0 and 1.

![InterPro Per-Protein Coverage Distribution Example](query_ipr_longest_domain_coverage_distribution.png)

#### How to interpret
- **Violin shape** shows the density of coverage values at each level.
  Most well-annotated proteomes are bimodal: a peak at 0 (proteins with
  no IPR hit) and a peak near 1 (single-domain proteins fully covered
  by their domain).
- **Box overlay** shows the IQR and median (white line); the white
  diamond marks the mean.
- **Stats line** below the plot reports n, mean, median, and the count
  of zero-coverage proteins per species — the latter is often the most
  diagnostic single number for annotation quality.
- **Query species** appears at the right with a red border and is
  separated from the reference set by a dashed grey line.

## Pipeline Processes

| Process                    | Description                                                       |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| FASTA_TO_JSON              | Converts FASTA → Protenix JSON                                    |
| SPLIT_JSON                 | Splits JSON into chunk files                                      |
| PROTENIX_PREDICT           | Runs Protenix inference (GPU)                                     |
| COLLECT_CHUNKS             | Merges chunk prediction outputs                                   |
| PROCESS_MODELS             | Extracts pLDDT values into PKL                                    |
| PLOT_PLDDT                 | Generates structure confidence plots (disorder scatter needs Metapredict) |
| METAPREDICT_DISORDER       | Runs disorder prediction (GPU)                                    |
| PLOT_METAPREDICT           | Generates disorder comparison plots                               |
| PSAURON_RUN                | Runs PSAURON scoring (GPU)                                        |
| PLOT_PSAURON               | Generates PSAURON overlay distribution plots                      |
| CHUNK_IPR                  | Splits FASTA into length-balanced InterProScan chunks (LPT)       |
| INTERPROSCAN               | Runs InterProScan on each chunk                                   |
| CONCAT_IPR                 | Merges per-chunk XML/TSV results                                  |
| PLOT_INTERPRO              | Generates InterPro coverage comparison plots                      |
| GENERATE_REPORT            | Combines per-branch PNGs into the final PDF report                |
| BUILD_SUMMARY_TSV          | Writes the single-row summary TSV; columns for skipped branches are blank |
| PLOT_PLDDT_COMBINED        | pLDDT plots with every input together (`--report combined`)       |
| PLOT_METAPREDICT_COMBINED  | Disorder density with every input together (`--report combined`)  |
| PLOT_PSAURON_COMBINED      | PSAURON categories with every input together (`--report combined`) |
| PLOT_INTERPRO_COMBINED     | InterPro coverage plots with every input together (`--report combined`) |
| GENERATE_COMBINED_REPORT   | Builds `<combined_name>_report.pdf` from the combined plots       |
| COMBINE_SUMMARY_TSV        | Joins the per-input summary rows into `<combined_name>_summary.tsv` |

## 是什么

这是一个针对帕金森病相关蛋白 alpha-synuclein 纤维的分子对接计算实验仓库。它使用 AutoDock Vina 对 58 个化合物（8 个已知结合剂 + 50 个无关药物）进行对接，检验标准对接流程能否区分已知结合剂与诱饵分子。仓库同时包含一个独立的 ESM-2 蛋白语言模型分析，比较家族性突变对接触图的影响。

## 亮点

- **严谨的阴性对照设计**：包含重对接对照（apo 和 holo 受体）、对称性感知的 RMSD 计算、以及家族突变 vs 对照突变的比较，避免将噪声误报为发现。
- **可复现性**：所有参数、随机种子、每姿态 RMSD 记录在 `results/summary.json`，PDB 文件运行时下载，不提交大文件。
- **自检机制**：`test_pipeline.py` 覆盖 8 个关键逻辑（对称 RMSD、统计方向、盐去除等），防止静默错误。
- **环境隔离**：分离 conda 环境避免 PyTorch 与 RDKit/Vina 的 OpenMP 冲突。
- **诚实报告**：明确列出限制（非结合亲和力、刚性受体、无溶剂），并引用相关文献（SymDOCK、CORAL）说明方法学背景。

## 为何对本课题有用

- **IDR/IDP 互作建模**：alpha-synuclein 是典型的固有无序蛋白，其纤维化与 LLPS 相关。仓库展示了如何用 cryo-EM 结构定义结合位点，并处理纤维对称性导致的重复位点问题——这对 IDP 纤维或相分离组装体的对接模拟有直接借鉴意义。
- **计算与 AI 方法评估**：ESM-2 接触图分析展示了如何用蛋白语言模型评估突变效应，并强调对照突变的重要性。这为 IDP 构象系综或突变功能预测提供了可迁移的评估框架。
- **物理模拟方法**：Vina 对接流程的失败案例（无法区分已知结合剂）提示了 IDP 纤维结合中配体-配体堆叠效应的重要性，可启发引入更高级的采样或评分方法（如 SymDOCK 的对称性感知评分）。

## 怎么用

- **主入口**：`run_pipeline.py`（完整对接流程，约 50 分钟），`src/esm_mutants.py`（ESM-2 分析）。
- **安装**：两个 conda 环境，见 `environment.yml`（RDKit, OpenBabel, Vina, Meeko）和 `environment-esm.yml`（PyTorch, ESM）。
- **输入**：PDB 7YNM（运行时下载），化合物 SMILES 从 PubChem 解析（`src/library.py`）。
- **输出**：`results/docking_results.csv`（每化合物 Vina 分数、配体效率）、`results/enrichment.csv`、`results/summary.json`、`results/figures/`。
- **GPU 需求**：ESM-2 分析需要 GPU（150M 模型约 0.59 GB），对接部分 CPU 即可。
- **调试**：`test_pipeline.py` 提供 8 个自检，`notebooks/results.ipynb` 提供结果可视化。

## 核心 idea

核心方法学洞察是：**在评估计算对接或 AI 预测方法时，必须包含严格的阴性对照和对称性感知的评估指标，否则结果可能只是伪影**。仓库通过重对接对照（apo vs holo）和家族突变 vs 对照突变的比较，揭示了 Vina 评分对分子大小的依赖（r²=0.47）和配体堆叠效应的重要性，从而证明标准对接流程不适用于纤维结合位点。

## 可搬移点

- **对称性感知的 RMSD 计算**（`src/dock.py`）：可解耦并移植到任何涉及重复结合位点的对接或构象评估 Pipeline 中，用于处理 IDP 纤维或对称组装体。
- **对照突变分析框架**（`src/esm_mutants.py`）：可复制用于 IDP 突变效应评估，确保结论不是由任意替换引起的。
- **环境隔离策略**：分离 PyTorch 和 RDKit/Vina 环境的 conda 配置，可复用于其他需要混合 AI 和分子模拟的 Pipeline。

readme:
# Docking small molecules against an alpha-synuclein fibril

A small, self-contained computational experiment on alpha-synuclein, the protein
that aggregates into fibrils in Parkinson's disease. It asks one question that
can actually be answered with the tools at hand:

> Can a standard AutoDock Vina setup, aimed at a binding site on alpha-synuclein
> that was **observed experimentally by cryo-EM**, tell published
> alpha-synuclein binders apart from unrelated approved drugs?

**The answer is no.** That is the result, and this repository is built to show
how it was reached rather than to dress it up.

The whole thing runs end to end on a laptop in about 50 minutes.

---

## The headline numbers

| Check | Result | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| **Redocking control** (apo receptor, the one used for the screen) | top-ranked pose **9.43 Å** from the crystal pose; best of 9 poses 6.25 Å | Fails the conventional 2 Å mark badly. The setup cannot rebuild a pose that was already measured. |
| **Redocking control** (neighbouring dye molecules kept) | top-ranked pose **8.04 Å**; best of 9 poses **2.79 Å** (ranked 7th) | A near-native pose is *generated*, but Vina's scoring does not rank it first. |
| **Known binders vs. decoys**, by Vina score | ROC AUC **0.67**, one-sided p = 0.064 | A weak trend, not significant at the 0.05 level with 8 references. |
| **Known binders vs. decoys**, by ligand efficiency | ROC AUC **0.44**, p = 0.73 | The trend **disappears** once molecular size is accounted for. |
| **Score vs. molecular size** | r² = **0.47**, p = 3e-09 | Nearly half the variance in the score is explained by how many atoms a molecule has. |
| **Thioflavin T**, the compound resolved bound in this exact site | ranks **41st of 58** | The one compound known to bind here scores worse than most unrelated drugs. |

The single most informative line is the last one. Thioflavin T is in the
structure, in this site, in the deposited coordinates. The protocol ranks it
below risperidone, tadalafil and prednisone.

![reference vs decoy](results/figures/reference_vs_decoy.png)

The apparent enrichment on raw score (left) does not survive normalising for
molecular size (right).

Ligand efficiency has a bias of its own, in the opposite direction: dividing by
heavy-atom count over-rewards very small molecules, and the top of that ranking
is metformin at 9 heavy atoms. So the two columns bracket the problem rather
than settling it — raw score favours large molecules, efficiency favours small
ones, and the reference compounds are not consistently at the top of either.
Neither metric is the arbiter on its own; what matters is that the apparent
signal does not survive a change of normalisation.

---

## Why this receptor and this site

Alpha-synuclein has no classical drug-binding pocket, so the tempting move is to
pick any fibril structure and choose a plausible-looking groove. A site chosen
that way cannot be checked. This uses **PDB [7YNM](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/7YNM)**
instead: a cryo-EM alpha-synuclein fibril with **Thioflavin T resolved in its
binding channel** — eight copies of it, stacked in two columns along the fibril
axis, spaced ~4.8 Å apart.

Picking a structure that already contains a ligand buys two things:

1. The docking box sits on a site someone measured, not on a guess.
2. There is a pose to check the protocol against — the redocking control above.

The box is built around the central dye copy and spans the groove lined by
**Tyr39, Glu46, Lys80, Thr81 and Val82**.

### The fibril symmetry problem

An amyloid fibril stacks identical subunits every ~4.8 Å, so the binding site
repeats along the fibril axis. **Three symmetry-equivalent copies of the site
fall inside the docking box**, and no practical box avoids this.

A pose that lands one layer over is the *same* binding mode, so scoring it
against one arbitrary copy reports a large RMSD for a correct answer. Every
pose here is therefore scored against **all eight deposited copies**, taking the
minimum. This was not a cosmetic choice: it was the first explanation tested for
the failing control, and it is worth stating that it did **not** rescue it — the
pose is genuinely ~8–9 Å away from every copy.

### Thioflavin T binds as a stack

The second explanation tested: Thioflavin T stacks along the fibril, so part of
each site's wall is built from its own neighbours, not from protein. Stripping
all eight copies deletes real binding surface.

So the control is run against two receptors:

- **apo** — every dye molecule removed. This is what the screen uses, because a
  drug would have to bind a fibril with no dye in it.
- **holo** — neighbours kept, one slot emptied.

Keeping the neighbours improves the score by ~3.5 kcal/mol and brings the best
generated pose to 2.79 Å. It still does not put that pose first. Both
explanations were real effects; neither fixed the problem.

---

## The library

58 compounds, every SMILES resolved from **PubChem by name** and checked against
a molecular formula recorded in the source, so a bad lookup raises instead of
quietly docking the wrong molecule.

**8 reference compounds** with published evidence of binding alpha-synuclein or
altering its aggregation — Thioflavin T, anle138b, EGCG, SynuClean-D, curcumin,
baicalein, fasudil and Congo red.

**50 decoys**: approved drugs from unrelated therapeutic areas.

Lipinski rule-of-five descriptors are computed and reported per compound, but
nothing is excluded on them — 4 of the 58 violate more than one rule, and they
are left in so the table shows what a filter would have removed. Descriptors are
computed on the desalted molecule, the same fragment that is docked, so a
counterion cannot inflate the heavy-atom count that ligand efficiency divides by.

Where the references actually landed:

| Rank (of 58) | Compound | Vina score | Ligand efficiency |
|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | Congo red | −8.12 | −0.176 |
| 3 | epigallocatechin gallate | −7.26 | −0.220 |
| 7 | anle138b | −6.92 | −0.330 |
| 11 | SynuClean-D | −6.59 | −0.264 |
| 24 | baicalein | −6.13 | −0.307 |
| 28 | curcumin | −5.91 | −0.219 |
| 41 | **Thioflavin T** | −5.34 | −0.267 |
| 53 | fasudil | −4.41 | −0.221 |

Congo red tops the table at 46 heavy atoms — the largest molecule in the set.
Given r² = 0.47 between score and size, that is the expected position for the
biggest molecule, not evidence of binding.

![ranked library](results/figures/ranked_library.png)
![size confound](results/figures/size_confound.png)

---

## Side analysis: ESM-2 contact maps for the familial mutants

Independent of the docking. Does a protein language model predict different
residue contacts for **A30P, E46K and A53T**, the point mutations that cause
familial Parkinson's disease — *more* than it does for substitutions that cause
nothing?

Sequence is UniProt **P37840** (140 aa), verified byte-for-byte against the
UniProt record, with each mutation site checked before substitution.

A bare "the maps barely change" would mean nothing — *any* single substitution
in a 140-residue protein barely changes them. So three **control
substitutions** with no reported Parkinson's link are run alongside, as a
baseline for how much an arbitrary mutation moves the map.

| | Variant | Map correlation to WT | Embedding cosine | Largest single change | Frobenius norm of change |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| familial | A30P | 0.9969 | 0.99973 | 0.181 | 0.766 |
| familial | E46K | 0.9949 | 0.99939 | 0.299 | 0.986 |
| familial | A53T | 0.9983 | 0.99988 | 0.166 | 0.571 |
| control | A19G | 0.9976 | 0.99987 | 0.212 | 0.687 |
| control | V40A | 0.9961 | 0.99991 | **0.365** | 0.854 |
| control | T75S | 0.9987 | 0.99994 | 0.260 | 0.495 |

**Median change — familial 0.766, control 0.687.** Effectively the same. And
the single largest perturbation in the whole set belongs to **V40A, a control**,
not to any disease mutation.

**A clear negative.** ESM-2 at this scale does not distinguish the mutations
that cause familial Parkinson's disease from arbitrary single substitutions.
Without the controls this would have been reported as "the familial mutations
barely perturb the map", which sounds like a finding and is not one.

A caveat on the correlation and cosine columns: both are computed over the
whole matrix or a mean-pooled embedding, so they are dominated by what the
variants share with wild type and sit near 1 by construction. They are reported
for completeness, but the familial-vs-control comparison is what carries the
argument.

One sanity check does pass: the wild-type map is dominated by near-diagonal
contacts with almost no long-range structure, which is the correct behaviour for
an intrinsically disordered protein.

![ESM-2 contact maps](results/figures/esm_contact_maps.png)

Run with ESM-2 **150M**. The 650M weights are 2.6 GB; 150M is 0.59 GB and
sufficient for a qualitative comparison. Change `MODEL_NAME` in
`src/esm_mutants.py` to use the larger model.

---

## What this does not show

- **Not binding affinities.** A Vina score is a scoring-function output that
  happens to carry kcal/mol units. It is not a measured free energy and does not
  convert to one. No number here is a Kd or an IC50.
- **No experimental validation.** Nothing was tested against protein. No
  compound here has been shown to do anything to alpha-synuclein by this work.
- **The decoys are not confirmed non-binders.** They are drugs with no published
  alpha-synuclein interaction, which is not the same as a measured negative.
  Some may well bind.
- **Rigid receptor, no solvent.** No explicit water, no ions, no protein
  flexibility, no entropy beyond the scoring function's approximation.
- **One polymorph.** Alpha-synuclein fibrils are polymorphic. A different
  polymorph gives a different site and different numbers.
- **8 references is a small sample.** The confidence interval on an AUC from 8
  positives is wide, which is exactly why the p-value of 0.064 is reported
  rather than described as a trend toward significance.
- **Neither scoring column is unbiased.** Raw Vina score rises with molecular
  size; ligand efficiency over-corrects and favours very small molecules. They
  are reported together because they fail in opposite directions, not because
  either one is the right answer.

Given that the redocking control fails, the ranking results should be read as
**evidence about this protocol**, not as evidence about these compounds.

---

## Related work, and what this project rediscovered

After finishing, I went looking for literature on the failure mode above. It is
a known problem, and two pieces of work target it directly. Both are worth
reading before taking anything here as novel.

**[SymDOCK](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.10.27.564400v1)** —
Smith, Knight, Kormos, Pepe, Kunach, Diamond, Shahmoradian, Irwin, DeGrado and
Shoichet (bioRxiv, 2023). Ligands on tau fibrils form stacks that follow the
fibril's symmetry, and *interact more with each other than with the protein*.
SymDOCK applies the fibril's symmetry operation to each pose, rejects poses
that clash with their own image, and adds a ligand-ligand van der Waals term to
the score. It reproduces the poses of three tau PET tracers, and predicted the
MK-6240 stack before that structure was solved.

**[CORAL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17412)** — Sun, Li, Tao and Schmidhuber
(arXiv:2607.17412, 2026). A reinforcement-learning docking model whose reward
combines docking affinity with a *cooperative ligand-ligand stacking energy*
term, together with an expert-validated amyloid evaluation set. A recent
preprint; part of its benchmark uses generated rather than experimental
reference poses.

This reframes the results above. The apo-vs-holo comparison here — neighbouring
dye copies being worth 3.5 kcal/mol and taking near-native poses from 0/9 to
2/9 — is an independent rediscovery of the premise both methods are built on,
not a new finding. Equally, "Vina's scoring cannot rank the stacked pose first"
is close to the motivation for writing SymDOCK in the first place.

So the honest conclusion is narrower than it first looked: **plain AutoDock
Vina is the wrong tool for a ligand that binds in a symmetric stack**, and the
right tools already exist. What this repository contributes is a worked
demonstration of catching that with a control rather than shipping the rankings.

One concrete improvement those papers point to: SymDOCK enriches known ligands
over **property-matched** decoys. The decoys here are approved drugs from
unrelated areas, which are not matched for size or physicochemical properties —
and since score correlates with size at r² = 0.47, property matching would be a
materially better design.

---

## Reproducing it

Two environments, because PyTorch ships its own OpenMP runtime that aborts at
import when the conda `libomp` used by RDKit and Vina is already loaded
(`OMP: Error #15`). Separating them avoids the unsafe `KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK`
override.

```bash
# docking
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate asyn
python test_pipeline.py      # 8 self-checks, a few seconds
python run_pipeline.py       # ~50 min: downloads 7YNM, controls, 58 docks
```

```bash
# ESM-2 side analysis
conda env create -f environment-esm.yml
conda activate asyn-esm
python src/esm_mutants.py
```

`python run_pipeline.py --reanalyze` recomputes descriptors, statistics and
figures from the saved docking scores without redocking — useful after a fix to
the analysis code, since the 50 minutes is all in the docking.

Nothing is committed that should not be: the PDB file and the prepared receptor
are downloaded at run time into `data/`, which is gitignored. No model weights.

### Layout

```
src/receptor.py      fetch 7YNM, find the ligand site, build the box and receptors
src/library.py       PubChem resolution with formula checking, Lipinski descriptors
src/dock.py          3-D embedding, PDBQT via Meeko, Vina, symmetry-aware pose RMSD
src/analyze.py       ranking statistics, enrichment, figures
src/esm_mutants.py   ESM-2 contact maps for WT vs familial mutants
run_pipeline.py      the whole docking run
test_pipeline.py     self-checks for the logic that could fail silently
notebooks/results.ipynb   walkthrough of the saved results
results/             docking_results.csv, enrichment.csv, summary.json, figures
notebooks/archive/   the original 2024 notebooks, none of which ran
```

`results/summary.json` records the receptor, box, every docking parameter, the
random seeds and the per-pose RMSDs, so the numbers above can be traced back.

### The self-checks

`test_pipeline.py` covers the logic where a bug would produce plausible-looking
numbers rather than an error: the symmetry-aware RMSD (a pose must score 0
against itself), the direction of the ranking statistics (more negative scores
must give AUC > 0.5), salt stripping, ligand efficiency, enrichment arithmetic,
the Lipinski filter, and the guard that rejects a mutation applied to the wrong
residue.

---

## History

This started as five exploratory notebooks in 2024. **None of them ever ran end
to end** — the Vina install failed on macOS arm64, the ESM calls imported the
wrong `esm` package, ESM3 was gated behind a 401, and one model was trained on
docking scores as labels, so it could only have learned to imitate Vina.

They are kept in [`notebooks/archive/`](notebooks/archive/) with
[a note on exactly what was broken in each](notebooks/archive/README.md). Nothing
in them should be read as a result.

readme:
Ensemble-aware protein binder design with generative conformational models and differentiable molecular energetics.

## Overview CINDER is a research framework for ensemble-aware protein binder sequence design with differentiable molecular energetics. It is built to test one hypothesis: that ranking and optimising binder sequences using an **ensemble** of conformations, scored by a differentiable energy ([TMol](https://pypi.org/project/tmol/)), tracks binding better than scoring a single minimised structure. ```mermaid flowchart LR T[Target T] --> Q[Sequence policy] Q --> S[Binder sequence S] S --> P[Conformation model] T --> P P --> X[Ensemble X₁ … Xₖ] X --> U[TMol energy] U --> R[Ensemble reward] R --> Q ``` A sequence policy `q(S|T)` proposes binders; a conformation model `p(X|S,T)` draws K structures, tilted toward low energy by a guidance strength λ; the energy `U(X,S,T)` is computed deterministically; the average over the ensemble is the sequence's reward, and the policy is updated by REINFORCE. The energy, the conformation model, the sequence optimiser and the experiment machinery are separate components joined by typed interfaces, so they can be swapped independently. Everything is config-driven (YAML), seeded and tested, and the toy CPU path always runs without TMol. **Status and honesty.** This is a research prototype. The energy tracks measured binding on three SKEMPI complexes, but the ensemble has **not** been shown to beat a single packed structure, and no design has been experimentally validated. Each ingredient, and several pairings, are established prior art (see [Related work](#related-work)); the combination is a recombination of known parts, not a demonstrated novelty. Measured results and open questions: [docs/results.md](docs/results.md) and [TODO.md](TODO.md). ## Capabilities | Area | What you can do | Needs TMol | |---|---|---| | Scoring | Score a complex (interface, repulsion, strain, `hbond`, `elec`, `internal`, soft H-bond graph first/second shell), with exact coordinate gradients | yes | | Conformations | Langevin sampling with energy guidance in Cartesian, rigid-body (jump), torsion (phi/psi/chi) or combined spaces; ensembles around a packed mutant | yes (protein systems) | | Learned models | Conditional normalising flow, diffusion and flow matching, trained and guided on toy coordinates | no | | Mutation | Mutate binder residues and repack side chains (one packed pose per sequence, cached) | yes | | Sequence design | REINFORCE with categorical or autoregressive (coupled) policies, design-space constraints, entropy bonus | toy: no; protein: yes | | Exact-gradient design | Optimise expected energy on pairwise energy tables, plus baselines (best single, one-body, random search, greedy hill climb) | table build: yes | | Position proposal | Pick design positions from H-bond shells or interface contacts | yes | | Validation | Perturb-and-recover benchmarks, mutant and position scans, SKEMPI 2.0 comparison with measured ddG | yes | | Outputs | Metrics and sequence CSVs, per-position probabilities, checkpoints, PDB files, `config.yaml` and `metadata.json` per run | no | Not available yet: mutations in the target chain, BioEmu2 (stub), protein-scale learned models, torsion degrees of freedom inside the design loop, and anything on GPU that has been tested. ## Install ```bash conda activate cinder pip install -e ".[dev,tmol]" # drop ",tmol" for a CPU-only toy install cinder doctor # reports the environment and optional backends ``` ## Usage ### Command line ```bash cinder design --config configs/experiment/toy_design.yaml # toy S→X→U→R→S loop, CPU, seconds cinder design --config configs/experiment/design_tmol.yaml # barnase/barstar with TMol, minutes on CPU cinder score --config configs/experiment/score.yaml # score the native complex (TMol) cinder sample --config configs/experiment/sample.yaml # sample an ensemble, report energies cinder analyze runs/ # summarise a finished run ``` Every run writes `runs/_/` with `config.yaml`, `metadata.json`, `metrics.csv`, `sequences.csv`, `probabilities.csv` and checkpoints (benchmark scripts add `results.csv` and `structures/`). `runs/` and `data/` are git-ignored. ### Configuration An experiment is one YAML file with these sections (see `configs/` for complete examples): | Section | Choose with | Examples | |---|---|---| | `system` | `kind` | toy, or `structure` with a PDB path, `target_chains`, `binder_chains`, `design_positions`, `forbidden_aa` | | `energy` | `backend` | `toy_sequence`, `tmol` with per-term weights (`interface_weight`, `hbond_weight`, `elec_weight`, `hbond_graph_weight`, ...) | | `conformation` | `backend` | `langevin` (toy), `rigid_langevin` (TMol; `n_samples`, `guidance_strength`, `step_size`, `n_steps`, `init_std`) | | `sequence` | `backend` | `categorical`, `autoregressive`; `init: native` or `uniform` | | `optimization` | `aggregator` | `batch_size`, `learning_rate`, `iterations`; aggregator `mean`, `median`, `softmin`, `quantile`, `free_energy` | Setting `n_steps: 0, init_std: 0, n_samples: 1` reduces the ensemble to the single packed structure, which is the baseline for the ensemble comparison. `device: auto` uses a GPU when present (the default is CPU). Components and their interfaces are described in [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md). ### Scripts Scripts download public PDB entries into `data/` on first use. Run them from the repository root. | Script | Purpose | |---|---| | `scripts/structure_recovery.py` | displace the binder and test whether guided sampling recovers it (`--space {cartesian,rigid,torsion,torsion_rigid}`) | | `scripts/mutant_scan.py` | score a CSV of mutants with the single structure and with the ensemble | | `scripts/position_scan.py` | all 19 substitutions at interface positions, with the native residue's rank | | `scripts/random_mutants.py` | low-rate, interface-biased random mutants | | `scripts/mutate_refine.py` | noise the backbone, mutate, then refine by gradient descent | | `scripts/table_design.py` | pairwise tables, exact-gradient design, and baselines (`--shells {first,second,both,contact}`) | | `scripts/skempi_validation.py` | compare scores with measured SKEMPI 2.0 ddG (you supply `skempi_v2.csv`) | | `scripts/validation_report.py` | reproduce the verification tables (about a minute on CPU) | ```bash python scripts/structure_recovery.py --complex 2ZTA --space rigid --rot 0 2 --trans 0 1 --n 1 \ --steps 4000 --step-size 2e-5 --lam0 5 --lam1 50 --clip 2000 python scripts/skempi_validation.py --skempi skempi_v2.csv --entry 3SGB_E_I --subsample 100 python scripts/table_design.py --complex 1CDL --shells contact ``` SKEMPI 2.0 is not shipped; download it and check its terms of use. ### As a library ```python from cinder.config import config_from_dict from cinder.experiments.runner import run_design cfg = config_from_dict({"system": {"binder_length": 2}, "optimization": {"iterations": 120}}) result, run_dir = run_design(cfg) # toy S→X→U→R→S loop print(result.best_sequence, run_dir) ``` `config_from_dict` accepts the same nested keys as the YAML files; `build_components(cfg)` returns the energy, conformation model, policy and design space for custom loops. Runnable examples are in `examples/` (`01_score_complex.py`, `02_sample_langevin.py`, `03_optimize_sequence.py`). ### Tests and checks ```bash pytest # CPU tests (155), TMol/GPU/slow tests excluded by default pytest -m tmol # TMol tests (52, about five minutes) ruff check . && ruff format --check . && mypy src ``` ## Repository structure ``` src/cinder/ types.py config.py cli.py doctor.py systems/ design space, molecular system, rigid-body (jump) parametrization energy/ toy energies, composite, restraints, parametrized; tmol*.py (the only TMol imports) conformations/ Langevin, normalising flow, diffusion, flow matching (toy), guidance, BioEmu2 stub sequence/ categorical and autoregressive policies, design-space constraints objectives/ ensemble aggregators, H-bond graph, pairwise tables, regularisers optimization/ REINFORCE trainer, expected-energy optimiser, search baselines experiments/ runner, TMol reward and study, logging, checkpoints validation/ perturbations, recovery, mutation scans, SKEMPI, PDB fetch, checks scripts/ configs/ docs/ examples/ tests/ assets/ ``` ## Related work Prior art (not exhaustive): - Ensemble-aware binder design: [ProChoreo](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.01.23.701298.full.pdf), [AlloGen](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.05474). - Ensemble-averaged design with a Rosetta-family energy: [RosettaBackrub](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21789164/), [flexible-backbone benchmark on binding interactions](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6901717/), [Rosetta:MSF multistate design](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pcbi.1005600). - Energy-guided sequence design for complexes: [EnerBridge-DPO](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.09496). - Reinforcement learning for binders: [ProtRL](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.12979), [HighPlay](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.03.17.643626.full.pdf). - Boltzmann-style ensemble objectives for conformation generators: [energy-based alignment](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.24203). - Gradient-based sequence design over simulated ensembles (disordered proteins): [Nature Comput. Sci. 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43588-025-00881-y). - Energy/force-guided conformation sampling: [ConfDiff](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.14088v2), [energy-based diffusion Boltzmann generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02080). - Single-structure backpropagation objectives (BindCraft-style), reviewed in [AI-driven binder design](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/csbj.0070). - TMol itself: [IPD Rosetta reimplementation](https://pypi.org/project/tmol/). Not yet checked (those searches failed): differentiable-physics design through ensembles, and BioEmu-based design. A full literature review is required before any publication claim. ## Documentation [Results](docs/results.md) · [Theory](docs/theory.md) · [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) · [TMol](docs/tmol.md) · [Models](docs/models.md) · [Sequence optimisation](docs/sequence_optimization.md) · [H-bond graph](docs/hbond_graph.md) · [Validation](docs/validation.md) · [Development](docs/development.md) · [TODO](TODO.md) ## Citation See [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff). Test and benchmark structures are public RCSB PDB entries: barnase/barstar (1BRS; Buckle, Schreiber & Fersht, 1994), committed as a fixture, and 2ZTA, 1CDL and 1G5J, downloaded at run time. Teddymer (CC BY-NC 4.0) was considered and not used; see [docs/validation.md](docs/validation.md). ## License Apache-2.0.
